```{=html}
      <div><h3>Carry a compact state</h3><p>Each token updates a recurrent state and reads an output from it.</p><h3>Select what to retain</h3><p>Input-dependent B, C and Δ control writing, reading and state dynamics.</p><p>The recurrent state has fixed shape during inference; the block also keeps a short convolution state.</p></div>
```

::: {.notes}
We have just explored how architecture changes a model's computation. Now ask a different question: what if we keep the model and improve the material it learns from? DataComp-LM provides several levels of evidence that dataset design can improve model quality independently of architecture design.

**First click: CHANGE THE ARCHITECTURE, Figure 6 (Appendix I, PDF p.43), replotted as a dumbbell chart.** Each horizontal row represents one dataset used to train models at the 1B-1x scale. The three points give Core scores for Mamba (orange), OpenLM (white ring), and a Gemma-like Transformer (blue). Every point uses the same horizontal score axis. The connecting line spans these architecture results, rather than a confidence interval. Read within a row to compare architectures, then compare rows to see the differences between datasets.

**Optional architecture cards.** Select Mamba, OpenLM or Gemma-like in the chart legend. Each card explains the model used in this comparison. Close with Escape, the close button or the backdrop to resume the same slide and fragment. The OpenLM card reuses our decoder-only backbone from Architecture slide 1: token mixing is causal self-attention and the FFN uses SwiGLU. The Gemma-like card uses the same backbone with GeGLU highlighted in the FFN and a separate RMSNorm annotation. Appendix I confirms RMSNorm inclusion but does not specify its exact placement, so the Norm labels stay generic. The Mamba card reuses Figure 3 from the Architecture lecture. The OpenLM and Mamba cards link to the corresponding slide.

All ten datasets from Figure 6 remain present: C4, RefinedWeb, RedPajama, Dolma v1, DCLM-baseline, and five other datasets grouped under “Ours (variants)” in the original legend. “Ours · variant 1” through “Ours · variant 5” are short presentation labels for those five distinct datasets. Rows are ordered by OpenLM score. These labels do not represent five repetitions of the same experiment. The full dataset identities and architecture scores are recorded in the accompanying figure data.

The higher-performing data preparation methods generally remain stronger across the tested architectures, although detailed rankings can change. Mamba's absolute scores are lower in this comparison. The near coincidence of OpenLM and Gemma-like on some rows also shows why three points may appear very close together. This supports transfer across these architectures, rather than identical absolute scores or a universal guarantee about every model.

The Gemma-like values come from the authors' architecture results CSV, and OpenLM values from their model database, using the original Core metric of the conference experiments. Mamba values are reconstructed from the original Figure 6 vector coordinates. They are paired with the same datasets through the shared OpenLM coordinates, so their precision is limited by the PDF. All thirty plotted scores have been matched to the published Figure 6.

**Second click: CHANGE THE DATA, Table 12 (Appendix H, PDF p.44).** Here we can make the controlled comparison. All three results use OpenLM at 1B-1x and the Default training recipe, with learning rate 3e-3 and weight decay 3.3e-2. This scale uses about 1.4B parameters and 28.8B training tokens. The Core scores are C4 23.7, RedPajama 25.7, and DCLM-baseline 30.2. Replacing the dataset improves the score by 6.5 points over C4 and 4.5 over RedPajama. These are points on the Core centered-accuracy metric, averaged over 22 tasks, rather than MMLU accuracy or relative percentage improvements. The horizontal bars start at zero.

**Third click: THE EFFECT PERSISTS.** Figure 3 (PDF p.5) compares the same data preparation methods at smaller scales with their performance at 7B-1x. In the conference version, the smaller scales are 400M-1x, 1B-1x and 3B-1x. The reported Pearson correlations are 0.838, 0.956 and 0.982 respectively. Dataset advantages do not necessarily vanish when scaling the model. This is evidence within the tested methods and scales, not a claim that rankings must stay fixed indefinitely.

The second lower graph is the MMLU 5-shot panel of Figure 1 (PDF p.2). It places DCLM-baseline in the wider context of quality and total training FLOPs. Its original logarithmic axis, point positions and model symbols are preserved. DCLM-baseline's diamonds and connecting line receive the lime accent. Other points are muted. This comparison includes different architectures and training recipes, so use it to illustrate practical compute efficiency, not as another strictly controlled architecture or dataset ablation. Keep its MMLU metric distinct from the Core scores in the other figures.

**Fourth click: Same model. Same budget. +6.5 Core. Where did it come from?** Keep this riddle open: the quality-classifier slide answers the first part, and the closing slide of the block answers the rest. The experiments suggest that designing training data is an independent source of model improvements. A natural next idea is to collect as much material as possible from the internet. The next slide asks why that alone is insufficient and introduces the seven data-design decisions in this lecture.

**Sources:** [Li et al., DataComp-LM: In search of the next generation of training sets for language models, NeurIPS 2024](https://papers.nips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/19e4ea30dded58259665db375885e412-Paper-Datasets_and_Benchmarks_Track.pdf), [authors' Gemma-like architecture results](https://github.com/mlfoundations/dclm/blob/361714bdd60bb9b7f4b2d8354cebbf0dec0c329e/assets/architecture_results_gemma_like.csv), and [authors' model database](https://github.com/mlfoundations/dclm/blob/361714bdd60bb9b7f4b2d8354cebbf0dec0c329e/assets/DCLM_model_database.csv). Figure and table numbering follows the conference PDF. Figure 6 uses a new composition with a shared Core score axis. Figures 3 and 1 retain their original vector geometry. The Table 12 bars use the exact Default rows.
:::

::: {.notes}
We have just seen that changing training data can substantially change model quality. A natural idea follows: gather as much material as possible from the internet, put it in a giant dataset, train the model, and deploy it. The diagram on the left deliberately makes this look straightforward. Web pages, books, code, PDFs, images, videos, and forums all feed one container.

**First click: show only the cartoon image.** The supplied cartoon appears on the right as a visual reaction to the naive approach. The existing diagram stays unchanged at full contrast; no heading, caption, or question mark appears on this click. Volume alone does not guarantee a useful training set. We must decide what experience the model should receive and which abilities that experience should build.

**Second click: replace the image with the lecture roadmap.** The naive approach now dims, the question mark appears, and the map is headed WHAT ACTUALLY MATTERS? The eight cards form two columns of four, read row by row. We begin with Sources & tokens at the top left: where training examples come from, how we prepare them, and how different modalities become model inputs.

The next six cards introduce related data-design directions. Data mixtures ask which sources to use and how often to present them. Filtering and deduplication ask which records to keep. Synthetic data asks which new examples to create. Long-context data asks how to make learning depend on information spread across a long input. Interaction trajectories ask how to capture actions and their outcomes. Safety data asks which behavior to reinforce. The final card at the bottom right is Part II: after the text conclusion, we apply the same rules to images and video.

This is a roadmap for the lecture, not a fixed processing pipeline. The six design directions are related: synthetic examples may also be filtered or used to teach safe behavior. The icons identify topics; they do not encode measurements or a ranking.

The emphasis now belongs to the decisions on the right. Building a training set includes managing its composition, quality, exposure frequency, new examples, and learning tasks. This is the roadmap for the lecture.

We begin with **SOURCES & TOKENS**. The next slide asks whether we can simply download the web: which pages are worth learning from, which we may use, and what they would teach. We then examine sources, the meaning of data dates, and the representations used for text, images, video and audio. Before **DATA MIXTURES**, three experiments ask why scale matters, why repetition has limits, and how selection changes training efficiency.
:::

::: {.notes}
**Initial state — JUNK.** The naive recipe was “download everything”. Look at what that actually collects: menus, a sale banner, a trending sidebar, a spam comment and a cookie prompt surround a small useful paragraph. The page is fictional, not a measured page composition. DataComp-LM starts with DCLM-Pool, 240 trillion tokens extracted from Common Crawl; the released DCLM-baseline has about 4 trillion tokens. The bars share a scale: 360 px versus 6 px, approximately 60:1. This reduction reflects the full curation pipeline, including language/quality filtering and deduplication, not just removing advertisements or a claim that 98% of every page is junk. Sources: [DataComp-LM, §3.1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.11794), [DCLM-baseline dataset card](https://huggingface.co/datasets/mlfoundations/dclm-baseline-1.0).

**Click 1 — WRITTEN BY AI.** The kettle reviews are invented teaching examples: one reads like a customer’s experience; two visibly retain model-response boilerplate. They are not a classifier or evidence for the fraction of the web written by AI. The distribution sketch illustrates loss of rare cases across generations. Shumailov et al. demonstrate model collapse under recursive training on model-generated data; the risk concerns indiscriminate reuse and loss of access to the original distribution. It is not a claim that all synthetic data is harmful. The curves are schematic, not digitized experimental measurements. Source: [Shumailov et al., Nature, 24 July 2024](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07566-y).

**Click 2 — STALE.** A crawl freezes a page at collection time. In this invented example, examplelib lists v4.2 in CC-MAIN-2026-43, October 2026. A later “today” page lists v5.0. Both version numbers and the package are illustrative; “today” is a later state in the story, not a release announcement. A model trained on the earlier snapshot sees v4.2 unless fresher data or retrieval updates its information. The crawl identifier is real; the library is not. Source: [Common Crawl statistics, CC-MAIN-2026-43](https://commoncrawl.github.io/cc-crawl-statistics/plots/languages).

**Click 3 — SOLD.** The two generic page mockups illustrate real commercial access arrangements without copying platform branding. Reuters reported in February 2024 that the Reddit–Google contract was worth approximately $60 million per year, attributed to a source; this is a reported estimate, not publicly disclosed contract terms. Stack Overflow announced an OverflowAPI partnership with Google Cloud on 29 February 2024 and an API partnership with OpenAI on 6 May 2024. The OpenAI price was not disclosed. Optional spoken context only: TechRadar reported suspensions of users who edited or deleted answers in protest. Avoid saying the site owns their copyright: the public terms describe a perpetual, irrevocable, non-exclusive licence, not a transfer of authorship. Sources: [Reuters syndication](https://www.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/exclusivereddit-in-ai-content-licensing-deal-with-google-sources-say-3310585), [SO × Google Cloud](https://stackoverflow.co/company/press/archive/google-cloud-strategic-gen-ai-partnership/), [SO × OpenAI](https://stackoverflow.co/company/press/archive/openai-partnership), [TechRadar, 9 May 2024](https://www.techradar.com/pro/stack-overflow-bans-users-for-altering-answers-to-protest-openai-deal), [Stack Overflow public terms, §6; current wording checked 28 October 2026](https://stackoverflow.com/legal/terms-of-service/public).

**Click 4 — OPTED OUT.** The invented robots.txt blocks GPTBot, CCBot and Google-Extended while leaving a general Allow rule for other agents. Google-Extended is a product-use control token, not a separate HTTP crawler identity; the “Gemini training” annotation is abbreviated. This file is a teaching mockup, not the observed policy of a named site. Longpre et al.’s 2023–24 audit reports roughly 5%+ of all C4 tokens, or 28%+ of the most actively maintained critical C4 sources, fully restricted. These are different denominators and a historical observation, not current shares for the whole web. Do not confuse these figures with the paper’s separate 45% terms-of-service statistic. Source: [Consent in Crisis, NeurIPS 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.14933).

**Click 5 — PERSONAL.** Every profile field is fictional: the .example email, 555-0142 phone number, name, address and silhouette are placeholders. The adjacent incident is real. In September 2022, a patient using the name Lapine reported finding her postoperative medical-record images referenced in LAION-5B. Ars Technica confirmed the case and found thousands of similar patient-record photographs. LAION is an index of links and captions, rather than a host of all the images. An indexed URL does not by itself establish whether a particular released model trained on that image. Sources: [Ars Technica original report](https://arstechnica.com/information-technology/2022/09/artist-finds-private-medical-record-photos-in-popular-ai-training-data-set/), [AI Incident Database #465](https://incidentdatabase.ai/cite/465/).

**Click 6 — HARMFUL.** Show only abstract, redacted index rows: these are not real URLs, captions or images. Stanford Internet Observatory identified 3,226 suspected CSAM entries in LAION-5B, with 1,008 externally validated as CSAM or likely CSAM (825 + 183 in Tables 2–3). The latter is a subset, not an additional count, and the report describes detection limits. LAION took LAION-5B and LAION-400M offline in December 2023 for review. The stamp marks that historical withdrawal, not a statement that all subsequent releases remain unavailable. Sources: [David Thiel, Stanford Internet Observatory report, corrected 23 December 2023; primary report mirrored by the US House](https://docs.house.gov/meetings/JU/JU08/20240306/116913/HHRG-118-JU08-20240306-SD005-U5.pdf), [LAION statement, 19 December 2023](https://laion.ai/notes/laion-maintenance/), [404 Media on the two withdrawn datasets](https://www.404media.co/laion-datasets-removed-stanford-csam-child-abuse/).

**Click 7 — SKEWED.** These are primary-language shares of crawled HTML pages in CC-MAIN-2026-43, not token shares, speaker populations, or a representative census of the entire web. English 42.56%; Russian 6.30; German 5.77; Japanese 4.89; French 4.76; Spanish 4.74; Chinese 4.37; Italian 2.58; Portuguese 2.47; Polish 1.89; Dutch 1.75; Czech 1.15. English is the largest group, below an absolute majority, hence the precise scene heading. Recounting the official CSV gives 161 named language labels, of which 123 are below 0.1%. The site’s prose says the detector supports 160 languages, but the actual crawl CSV has 161 labels; use the observed denominator. The unknown category (3.0552%) is omitted from the graphic without renormalizing the other percentages. Source: [Common Crawl language statistics](https://commoncrawl.github.io/cc-crawl-statistics/plots/languages), [official CSV](https://commoncrawl.github.io/cc-crawl-statistics/plots/languages.csv); saved extract in validation/data_d03_20261028/languages-2026-43.json.

**Click 8 — LEAKED TESTS.** A fictional forum shows an abridged genuine GSM8K test problem: John has three boxes with outside dimensions 5 × 6 × 4 inches and 1-inch walls. Inside each is 3 × 4 × 2 = 24 cubic inches; three boxes give 72. The requested Natalia problem also has answer 72 but is in the training split, so it was replaced to keep the “test set” label accurate. The forum is an illustration of possible leakage, not a documented contaminated training example. GSM1k is a fresh, matched arithmetic benchmark. The published NeurIPS 2024 version reports accuracy drops of up to 8%, not the earlier preprint’s 13%. Bars are schematic and do not encode absolute accuracies. This comparison is evidence consistent with overfitting in some models, not proof every model memorizes benchmarks; many frontier models show little evidence of overfitting. Sources: [GSM8K official test data](https://github.com/openai/grade-school-math/blob/master/grade_school_math/data/test.jsonl), [Zhang et al., NeurIPS 2024](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/hash/53384f2090c6a5cac952c598fd67992f-Abstract.html).

**Click 9 — TAKEAWAY.** “Downloading is the easy part.” All nine examples have asked three simple questions: is it worth learning from, is it ours to take, and what would it teach? Now broaden the source map to text, images, audio and video. All page designs, domains, personal fields and review snippets are teaching mockups; the cited measurements and incidents are real, with the scope described above.

:::

::: {.notes}
Bridge from D 03: downloading the web leaves questions about quality, permission, privacy, harm, representation and test leakage. Now broaden the source map to all four modalities. These clouds combine source platforms and archives with named example corpora, so the source map also gives concrete collections to look up. They are not a global ranking or the undisclosed recipe of a commercial model. Font sizes provide visual emphasis only.

Text is visible initially. Dolma Table 1 and §§5–8 document web pages via Common Crawl, GitHub code, Reddit discussions, Semantic Scholar papers, Project Gutenberg books and Wikipedia. Common Crawl is an archive used for collection; the original material comes from web pages. Additional corpus labels are C4, The Stack, peS2o and Dolma; Wikibooks adds another documented source. These are collections at different stages, not independent non-overlapping origins.

First click — images. LAION-5B §3 uses image URLs and alt-text discovered through Common Crawl. Its §2 also describes image–text corpora from Flickr (YFCC100M), Reddit (RedCaps), and Wikipedia (WIT). The expanded cloud also names LAION-5B, YFCC100M, RedCaps, WIT, MS-COCO, CC3M, CC12M and Visual Genome from Table 1 and §2. WIT here means Wikipedia Image Text. These are examples across corpora, not a list of the most frequent websites within LAION.

Second click — audio. WavCaps §III-A brings together Freesound, BBC Sound Effects, SoundBible and an AudioSet subset; AudioSet's underlying clips come from YouTube. LibriSpeech adds read speech from LibriVox audiobooks. The cloud also names WavCaps, AudioSet, LibriSpeech, AudioCaps and Clotho as example corpora; WavCaps §§II–III describe the captioning collections. Audio therefore includes speech, music and environmental sounds, not just transcripts.

Third click — video. HowTo100M uses instructional YouTube videos; WebVid uses stock-video sites, as explicitly identified in the [authors' repository](https://github.com/m-bain/webvid); see also [Frozen in Time §4.1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.00650). The comparison tables include movie datasets and home recordings; Charades documents people recording everyday actions at home. Frozen in Time Table 1 adds Flickr and names DiDeMo, MSR-VTT, ActivityNet and LSMDC alongside WebVid, HowTo100M and Charades. These corpora include pretraining and task-specific training/evaluation collections; the cloud does not claim that they all serve the same role. These sources offer different kinds of scenes and actions.

The point is to choose a source mix for the intended skills and coverage, then assess the source against the questions from D 03 before preparing training examples. The next slide asks how old the collected material is: publication, collection and model-release dates need not coincide.

**Reserve — consent, training use and retention.** The former main-slide example is retained here. For one voice recording, ask three separate questions: who agreed to which purpose; whether training or evaluation is allowed; which objects are stored and under what deletion rules. One answer does not determine the other two. See [Datasheets for Datasets](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.09010).

**Reserve — service/API documentation examples.** Optional material only, not part of the main slide sequence. The snapshot below was checked on 21 October 2026; consult the linked current documentation before presenting exact policy details. Paid/unpaid classification can depend on region, billing and account context.

Gemini voice replication requires reference and consent audio. The two TTLs apply to specific custom-voice objects: stateful voice_ profiles last one year since their most recent use; client-managed stateless voicekey_ values last seven days. Active synthesis or use as a remix base extends the stateful TTL. Neither value describes all service request logs.

Under Gemini paid-service terms, prompts and responses are not used to improve products; limited logging for abuse prevention, security and legal/regulatory obligations remains. Unpaid-service treatment differs. In the EEA, Switzerland and UK, the paid data-use terms also apply to unpaid services; active billing and enterprise account context also affect the classification. Check the exact service and account, not just a free/paid UI label.

ElevenLabs Zero Retention Mode is available for selected enterprise customers and eligible endpoints, enabled on request. It limits logging of eligible API request/response data and is not a promise about all web-interface or other submitted data. The boundary represents scope, not a universal guarantee. This is a documentation framework, not a legal conclusion about identifiability or every jurisdiction.

Sources (checked 21 October 2026): [Gemini terms, 23 Mar 2026](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/terms); [Gemini custom voice TTL](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/speech-generation); [ElevenLabs ZRM](https://elevenlabs.io/docs/eleven-api/resources/zero-retention-mode).
:::

::: {.notes}
The gaps are intentional: a cutoff is not a promise of complete coverage before that date. The historical GPT-4 technical report says the vast majority of pretraining data ended in September 2021 and notes a small amount of more recent data. This is a 2023 example, not a claim about today's models.

Fine-tuning may use documents with another date distribution. Retrieval introduces an external source into the current input; ordinary reading does not mechanically rewrite model weights. Ask students: ‘Would a release date prove that the model knows last week's election result?’ A recent retrieved document helps, but relevance, reliability and the generated answer still need checking. Source publication, collection and model release dates describe different events. Vendors can use ‘training cutoff’ and ‘knowledge cutoff’ differently; read the individual model card.

Sources (checked 21 October 2026): [GPT-4 technical report §5 / footnote 10](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2303.08774); [RAG Figure 1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2005.11401).
:::

```{=html}
<title id="d06-title">Tokens are learned from data.</title>
<desc id="d06-description">Train character-level BPE independently on an English phrase and its Russian translation, with three merges each. Count pairs within words; exclude spaces. English: the fat cat sat with the rat has 22 letters. Merge a plus t four times, t plus h three times, then th plus e twice: 22, 18, 15, 13 tokens. Russian: толстый кот сидел с крысой also has 22 letters. All neighbouring pairs occur once. Break frequency ties by choosing the leftmost pair: т plus о to то, то plus л to тол, тол plus с to толс. Counts: 22, 21, 20, 19. Final comparison: 13 English tokens versus 19 Russian tokens after the same three-merge budget. The difference reflects repetitions in these specific phrases, not a universal property of either language.</desc>

```

::: {.notes}
**Initially — 22 tokens; bridge from D 03.** Recall SKEWED: the Common Crawl snapshot shown on D 03 was about 43% English. The language mix can affect not only what a model learns, but also the vocabulary learned by its tokenizer. Use one tiny training corpus: “the fat cat sat with the rat”. Use the same character-level BPE algorithm and three-merge budget for two independent training runs, one on each phrase. Each run starts with its own character alphabet. First train on the English phrase, then repeat training from scratch on its Russian translation. Initially each letter is one token: 22 in total. Spaces mark word boundaries; in this teaching example they are excluded from both pair counts and token counts, and no end-of-word marker is added. Count neighbouring pairs inside words across the whole phrase. Tokenizer training is separate from language-model training: it learns a vocabulary and an ordered merge list from a selected corpus.

**Click 1 — a + t → at; 18 tokens.** The pair occurs in fat, cat, sat and rat: four occurrences, the unique most frequent pair. Replace all four with at; 22 − 4 = 18. Only the four newly merged chips are lime. The first rule appears in the list and stays there. The letters keep their positions so the audience can see which boundaries disappear.

**Click 2 — t + h → th; 15 tokens.** Recount pairs after the first merge. This pair occurs in the, with and the: three occurrences, again the unique maximum. Replace all three: 18 − 3 = 15. In particular, with is now [w] [i] [th], not one token. The earlier at chips remain merged but return to gray; only the new th chips are lime. Add the second rule to the ordered list.

**Click 3 — th + e → the; 13 tokens.** Recount again: th + e occurs twice, in the two instances of the, and wins without a tie. Now 15 − 2 = 13. Read the result: [the] [f][at] [c][at] [s][at] [w][i][th] [the] [r][at]. Stop at the teaching budget of three merges. There are no ties for the winning pair in these three English steps; the Russian run will have ties and use an explicit leftmost-pair rule. Each resulting token has an integer vocabulary ID; IDs are labels, not magnitudes. The model uses those IDs to look up learned embedding vectors. Increasing the merge budget usually shortens sequences while growing the vocabulary and its embedding/output tables.

**Click 4 — train independently on Russian; 22 tokens.** Start a second training run with the same character-level algorithm and three-merge budget on “толстый кот сидел с крысой”. Do not apply the English rules to Russian. Its words have 7 + 3 + 5 + 1 + 6 = 22 letters, initially 22 tokens. All 17 distinct within-word neighbouring pairs occur exactly once. Declare the deterministic tie-break: among equally frequent pairs, choose the first encountered in a left-to-right scan of the current corpus. Recount pairs after every merge, just as in English. Spaces remain excluded.

**Click 5 — т + о → то; 21 tokens.** Every pair has frequency 1; choose the leftmost pair, т + о at the start of толстый. One replacement removes one boundary: 22 − 1 = 21. The first word becomes [то][л][с][т][ы][й]. This is a frequency tie, not a linguistically preferred segmentation.

**Click 6 — то + л → тол; 20 tokens.** Recount the current token pairs: each still occurs once. The leftmost candidate is now то + л. Merge its one occurrence: 21 − 1 = 20. The first word becomes [тол][с][т][ы][й].

**Click 7 — тол + с → толс; 19 tokens.** Recount again. Every candidate still has frequency 1; choose the leftmost, тол + с. One occurrence gives 20 − 1 = 19. Stop after exactly three merges. The final sequence is [толс][т][ы][й] [к][о][т] [с][и][д][е][л] [с] [к][р][ы][с][о][й]. The arbitrary-looking толстый boundary illustrates that BPE follows pair counts and tie-breaking, not morphology.

**Click 8 — compare the two trained results; 13 versus 19 tokens.** Both phrases started with 22 letters. Each tokenizer learned three merges from its own phrase. English saved 4 + 3 + 2 = 9 positions, ending at 13; Russian saved 1 + 1 + 1 = 3, ending at 19. This compares two independently learned rule sets under the same algorithm, merge budget and counting convention. The English phrase was constructed with repeated at, th and the patterns; this Russian translation has no repeated neighbouring pair. The difference is about repetition in these tiny training corpora, not an intrinsic disadvantage of Russian or evidence about production multilingual tokenizers. Now freeze each learned vocabulary and its ordered rules; applying the respective tokenizer to its own training phrase reproduces the displayed segmentation without relearning pair counts.

**Click 9 — takeaway; bridge to D 07.** Tokens are learned from data — so the data decides what is cheap. The model consumes a sequence of token IDs and embeddings, rather than letters or words as linguistic units. At a fixed context budget, equivalent meanings can occupy different numbers of positions; more tokens also means more sequence processing and potentially higher token-based cost. The tokenizer-training mix need not match the language-model training mix, and later model-training examples do not automatically change a frozen vocabulary. Connect this back to the English-heavy web on D 03. Transition to D 07: images need their own representation as a sequence; next we turn image patches into vectors.

Sources: [Sennrich et al., 2016, BPE §3.2](https://aclanthology.org/P16-1162.pdf), for character-level BPE learning and application. The two tiny corpora, three-merge budget for each, leftmost-pair tie-break, and exclusion of spaces/end-of-word markers are explicit teaching choices. Reproduce both training traces and final token sequences with validation/tokenizer_d06_two_trainings_20261028/check_counts.py.
:::

```{=html}
<text x="1314" y="198" font-size="30" font-weight="600" fill="var(--fv-ink)" text-anchor="middle">…</text>
<rect x="1355" y="156" width="66" height="66" fill="var(--fv-soft)" stroke="var(--fv-line)"/>
<text x="1388" y="198" font-size="30" font-weight="600" fill="var(--fv-ink)" text-anchor="middle">v₁₆</text>
<text x="985" y="270" font-size="27" font-weight="400" fill="var(--fv-ink)" text-anchor="start">+ position for each patch</text>
<path d="M1205 289 L1205 321" fill="none" stroke="var(--fv-ink)" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#d07-arrow)"/>
<rect x="1065" y="340" width="280" height="66" fill="#fff" stroke="var(--fv-ink)"/>
<text x="1205" y="383" font-size="30" font-weight="600" fill="var(--fv-ink)" text-anchor="middle">Transformer</text>
<rect x="0" y="447" width="1488" height="73" fill="var(--fv-soft)" stroke="none"/>
<text x="18" y="472" font-size="25" font-weight="400" fill="var(--fv-ink)" text-anchor="start">224 × 224 pixels · 16 × 16 pixels per patch</text>
<text x="18" y="510" font-size="28" font-weight="600" fill="var(--fv-ink)" text-anchor="start">14 × 14 patches = 196 vectors</text>
<text x="820" y="490" font-size="27" font-weight="600" fill="var(--fv-ink)" text-anchor="start">Patch size sets sequence length.</text>
</g></svg></div>
<div class="fv-takeaway">One patch → one vector. More patches → a longer sequence.</div>
<div class="fv-source"><a href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2010.11929">ViT, Figure 1 and §3.1</a> · Original teaching diagram; vector values illustrative; class token omitted.</div>
```

::: {.notes}
**Bridge from D 06.** Text was converted to token IDs and then embeddings. Now ask how a two-dimensional image becomes a sequence of vectors. Show one concrete route: the input representation of a basic Vision Transformer (ViT). The cup is an original schematic drawing, not a model output.

**Initially:** one complete image of a cup. **Click 1 — cut into patches:** overlay a 4×4 grid and number the 16 equal squares in row order. A patch is a fixed-size region of pixels; the grid does not search for objects or cut out the whole cup. Patch 6 is outlined and numbered so its identity does not depend on color.

**Click 2 — encode each patch:** magnify exactly patch 6. Flatten its RGB pixels, then use the same learned linear projection for every patch to obtain D real-valued numbers. For a 16×16 RGB patch the input has 16×16×3 = 768 values; D is the chosen embedding width. The displayed [0.2, −0.7, …] is illustrative, not a computed output. In the original ViT this projection is trained jointly with the model. There is no separate BPE merge learning step or word-vocabulary lookup in this path. A pretrained vision encoder may later be frozen in a larger system.

**Click 3 — build the sequence:** line up v₁, v₂, …, v₆, …, v₁₆; add each patch's positional embedding before the Transformer. For a concrete input of 224×224 pixels and 16×16 patches there are 14×14 = 196 patch vectors. The original classification ViT adds a class token, giving 197 total positions; the slide counts only patch positions. For fixed patch size, doubling both input sides gives four times as many patches, provided that preprocessing actually preserves the larger input size. This is why image preprocessing changes sequence length.

**Reserve — compressed image representations.** The previous version of this slide compared image understanding and generation before establishing what a patch vector is. Keep the model-specific details here: in a spatial 3×3 merge, nine neighboring feature vectors can be moved into channels and projected, reducing a 6×6 grid to four sequence positions. This was linked to DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash's pixel-unshuffle description. It is not the basic ViT patch projection shown above. For generation, an encoder such as a VAE can first map an image into a smaller continuous latent grid; packing that grid is another step. The prior FLUX 3 demo reference uses AutoencoderKLFlux2, but the complete FLUX 3 packing path was not traced, so retain no total numerical compression claim. These are alternative representations, not extra steps that every image must pass through.

**Transition to D 08:** we have followed spatial regions in one image. Next, repeat the patch-to-vector step on selected video frames and retain their time positions.

Main source: [ViT, Figure 1 and §3.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2010.11929). Previous reserve references: [DeepSeek-V4.1, §2.1.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.19969v1); [FLUX 3 official demo](https://huggingface.co/spaces/black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein/blob/77e15faba0d6ef8d07ff53b5c19e256ef2ff757f/app.py). The 4×4 cup grid and example vector are original teaching choices.
:::


::: {.notes}
**Bridge from D 07.** We already know how one image produces patch vectors. Video repeats that operation across time: choose frames, make patches, and retain when each patch appeared. The example uses a simple frame-patch input representation, as in TimeSformer; it is not a claim that every video model uses this route.

**Initially — source video.** The original teaching clip shows the same cup moving right at 24 frames per second. The strip shows 25 consecutive frame instants from 0.0 s through 1.0 s, including both endpoints: 24 intervals of 1/24 s, not 25 fps. Treat this as a view into a longer clip, not as the ten-second counting example used later.

**Click 1 — sample frames.** Keep only A at 0.0 s, B at 0.5 s and C at 1.0 s; the other frames fade. These times identify selected moments in the source clip. The original FPS alone does not determine the input sequence length: the number of frames we select does. Selecting more frames preserves more temporal detail, but costs more tokens.

**Click 2 — patches.** Enlarge the three selected frames and split each into a deliberately coarse 2×2 grid. Read patches 1–4 in row order. The same cup moves right, so A2 and B2 refer to the same region at different times and can contain different pixels. Each patch becomes a continuous vector by the learned projection already explained in D 07; there is no new vocabulary-learning stage here. The toy grid is for readability, not the 16×16-pixel patch size of the later count.

**Click 3 — sequence.** Read A1–A4, then B1–B4, then C1–C4: 3 frames × 4 patches = 12 tokens. Each chip stands for one full vector. The patch number tells us where in the frame; the timestamp under its group tells us when in the clip. The model receives positional information along with the patch embeddings. A1…C4 are provenance labels, not vocabulary IDs. We omit the class token from all counts. Frame-major order is a display convention, not a claim about autoregressive generation or a universal internal tensor layout.

**Click 4 — scale at 224×224.** Now replace the toy clip with a ten-second example, using 16×16-pixel patches and no compression. Each frame has (224/16)×(224/16) = 14×14 = 196 patches. Keeping every frame at 24 fps gives 10×24 = 240 frames and 240×196 = 47,040 tokens. Keeping one frame per second gives ten frames and 10×196 = 1,960 tokens. The second bar is exactly 24 times shorter: 45.83 px when the first is 1,100 px. The interval is [0,10), so the 1 fps sample contains ten frame instants, not eleven. Resolution and selected-frame count jointly set sequence length.

**Click 5 — 4K60.** For ten seconds of UHD 3840×2160 at 60 fps, 16×16 patches give 240×135 = 32,400 patches per frame, about 165.3 times the 224×224 grid. Across 600 frames that is 19,440,000 tokens, or 1.944 million per second: about 413.3 times the 24 fps bar and 9,918.4 times the 1 fps example. At the same scale the bar would be 454,591.84 px, about 305.5 widths of our 1,488 px chart, hence “~300 slides.” Full attention over all tokens forms n² query–key pairs: 1,960² = 3,841,600 versus 19,440,000² = 377,913,600,000,000, a ratio of 98,374,010.8, or ~100M×. This is a full-attention pair-count comparison against the 224×224, 1 fps example, not a measured runtime or a claim about every video architecture. Uncompressed 8-bit RGB pixels alone use 3840×2160×3×600 = 14,929,920,000 bytes ≈ 14.93 GB (decimal), about 13.9 GiB; this is not model activation memory or a compressed video file. For intuition, 19.44 million tokens is about twenty 1M-token context windows. How do models work with video at all? TimeSformer separates temporal and spatial attention, while other video models reduce the sequence through a VAE and/or merging nearby patches. Use the reserve below for the MiniMax H3 and Sora examples.

**Click 6 — takeaway.** Raw video does not fit — models must sample and compress it. Sampling, resolution and representation compression are design choices, not incidental preprocessing: they decide how much temporal and spatial detail fits into the model input. The n² estimate applies only to full attention across all tokens; divided, local or other attention patterns change this cost.

**Reserve — compressed video representations.** The previous version of this slide used the MiniMax H3 description of a temporally causal f16t4d24 VAE: 16× spatial compression, 4× temporal compression and 24 feature channels, followed by 1×2×2 patchification. This gives an approximate spatial stride of 32 and N ≈ (H/32)(W/32)(T/4), away from boundary effects. A causal first frame, padding and rounding require checking the actual implementation. Channels are dimensions within a vector, not extra sequence positions. Those model-specific compression stages are not part of the simple frame-patch diagram above. The previous Sora reference illustrates another spacetime-patch route. Keep compression factors and API billing out of the main explanation.

**Transition to D 09:** video added time to the image representation. Audio also unfolds in time, but one audio frame can yield several discrete codes; the next slide explains that distinction.

Sources: [TimeSformer, §3, input patches and divided space-time attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.05095); [ViT, §3.1, patch embeddings and 16×16 patches](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.11929), checked 28 October 2026. Original cup illustration reused from D 08 / D 07; token, attention-pair and raw-pixel counts are teaching calculations, not benchmark measurements. Reserve sources: [MiniMax H3, H3-VisualVAE](https://huggingface.co/MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-H3); [Sora, spacetime patches](https://openai.com/index/video-generation-models-as-world-simulators/).
:::

```{=html}
<title id="d09-title">Audio frames become stacks of residual codes</title>

<div class="fv-source"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.03312">SoundStream (Zeghidour et al., 2021), residual vector quantizer</a> · <a href="https://huggingface.co/MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-Music3">MiniMax Music3 model card (25 frames/s, 8 codebooks)</a><span class="audio-credit">Original teaching diagram; 2D arrows illustrate how codes add up.</span></div>
```

::: {.notes}
**Initial state — waveform.** Video added time to images; audio is only time. We split the waveform into short frames. In this example the codec produces 25 frames per second, so one frame represents 1/25 s = 40 ms. The regular boundaries show time steps, not a claim that the encoder ignores neighboring sound.

**Click 1 — code 1, the rough sketch.** The codec encoder produces a vector for one frame; × marks that target. The first codebook selects its nearest entry. Its vector is the long arrow from the origin, and the index of that entry is code 1 in the stack. The gap to × is the residual: the original vector minus the chosen entry. This is a 2D teaching simplification; actual codec vectors have many dimensions.

**Click 2 — code 2, the first correction.** The second codebook quantizes the residual left by the first. Place that chosen vector at the tip of the first arrow: their sum is a better approximation to the frame vector. We emit one more index, code 2, and the residual indicator shrinks.

**Click 3 — codes 3 through 8.** Repeat on the remaining residual. The shorter arrows show successive corrections; the sum of the eight selected entries nearly reaches ×. We reveal these six small corrections together to keep the explanation moving. The final tiny residual is deliberately not zero. Arrow lengths and directions are illustrative, not measured MiniMax embeddings or a claim that every individual residual must shrink for every input.

**Click 4 — the matrix.** Each column is one 40 ms frame and each row is one codebook, from rough to fine. The outlined column contains eight discrete indices. Codebook 1 offers 16,384 entries; codebooks 2–8 offer 1,024 each. Vocabulary size is the number of choices in a codebook, not the number of codes emitted per frame. These are the MiniMax Music3 training-tokenizer settings, not universal audio settings.

**Click 5 — the scale.** For this 25 × 8 configuration, 25 frames/s × 8 codes/frame = 200 codes/s. A three-minute song gives 180 × 200 = 36,000 codes. An hour of speech, hypothetically encoded at this same rate, gives 3,600 × 200 = 720,000 codes. The speech example is a rate calculation, not a claim about Music3's supported speech use or one-hour generation. The phrase “close to a 1M-token context” is an order-of-magnitude comparison: codebook indices are not automatically one-for-one global Transformer positions. Other codecs use different frame rates and numbers of codebooks.

**Click 6 — takeaway.** Each audio frame becomes a stack of codes — rough first, then corrections — and the stacks add up fast. Bridge to Part I exp12 and the Training Talker discussion. The next data slide returns to the question of whether more data is always better.

**Sources and provenance.** [SoundStream (Zeghidour et al., 2021), §III-C and Algorithm 1, residual vector quantization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.03312); [MiniMax Music3 model card, Music Tokenizer and frame-rate setting](https://huggingface.co/MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-Music3), checked 28 October 2026. Original teaching diagram; 2D arrows illustrate how codes add up. Waveform, arrows and cell positions were drawn for this lecture; no third-party figure is reproduced.

**Reserve — billing.** Gemini TTS defines 25 billable audio tokens/s. This is a different counting system, not evidence that Gemini and MiniMax use the same codec. Source: [Gemini billing units](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/pricing).

**Reserve — MiniMax synthesis and backbone.** Keep the previous “Text Qwen · 8B” architecture explanation here: the [MiniMax Music3 model card](https://huggingface.co/MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-Music3) names Qwen3-8B, while the [MiniMax architecture blog](https://www.minimax.io/blog/minimax-music-3-0-next-generation-open-weights-production-ready-versatile-music-model) names Qwen3.5-8B; the sources disagree on the exact backbone version. Global modeling handles progression across frames; local modeling supplies acoustic detail within a frame. For inference, fused final hidden states feed Flow Matching and then Flow-VAE. The RVQ matrix teaches the training representation; waveform synthesis is not merely a discrete RVQ decoder.

**Reserve — separate Gemini example.** Gemini 3.8 Audio is based on Gemini 3 Pro, as stated in its [model card](https://deepmind.google/models/model-cards/gemini-3-8-audio/). Expressive output alone cannot establish these architectures. The old takeaway belongs here: “Audio frame rate, code rate, synthesis path and billing unit answer different questions.”
:::

## What we know so far {#data-recap-sources .fv-slide .data-recap-slide background-color="#ffffff"}

::: {.data-recap data-section="sources"}
:::

::: {.notes}
On opening, recall D 03: web access and usefulness are separate constraints, and DCLM shrinks from 240T to about 4T tokens (3.8T in Figure 4, shown on D 14). On click 1, D 04–05 remind us to choose sources for the skill and modality, because a cutoff date does not guarantee knowledge. On click 2, D 06–09 show the cost of representation: the D 08 calculation gives 19.44M tokens for ten seconds of uncompressed 4K60 with 16×16 patches, displayed as 19.4M. On click 3, connect the takeaway to D 02's question, “Where does data come from, and how does it become model input?” Collection and tokenization already constrain both learning and cost. Next, D 10 asks: “Do we really need more data?”
:::

::: {.notes}
The question is how to spend training compute when good new text is scarce. After the scale comparison, the first click moves directly to repetition; the second translates the fitted law into a concrete token-count example; the third moves to selection; the fourth connects the two and asks what to show and how often. Original figures remain intact; the FineWeb overlay highlights the comparison already described by its caption.

**Initial state: YES. SCALE MATTERS.** Paper Figure 1 plots compute-optimal parameter predictions against training FLOPs, both on logarithmic scales, alongside the actual model configurations. Gopher has 280B parameters and sees 300B tokens; Chinchilla has 70B parameters and sees 1.4T tokens (Table 1). Their training FLOPs are approximately the same. Table 6 reports 60.0% versus 67.6% MMLU 5-shot accuracy. These accuracy values annotate the graph; they are not plotted on its axes. More parameters are not always the best use of compute. The two models also differ in width, heads, optimizer (Adam vs AdamW), tokenizer and data mixture, so the comparison does not isolate token count (Hoffmann et al., §4.1, Table 4). The ⓘ cards beside Gopher and Chinchilla show both architectures and Table 4. Open them if students ask how the models differ beyond size.

**First click: OUT OF NEW DATA — CAN WE JUST REPEAT IT?** We need more training data, but good new text is limited. The first option is to reuse the same unique tokens. Figure 1 left from Muennighoff et al. shows 4.2B-parameter models. The horizontal axis gives processed training tokens and passes (epochs) over the same unique data; the vertical axis is final test loss, where lower is better. The dashed curve assumes repeats are as valuable as new data. The solid curve is the fitted repeated-data law; the points are measured runs. Follow 1, 4, 10, 40 and 100 passes. Original axes, points, inset, annotations and the left-panel legend are unchanged.

For unique tokens $U$ and extra passes $R=\text{epochs}-1$, the fitted effective-data law is $D'=U+U R_D^*(1-e^{-R/R_D^*})$, with $R_D^*=15.387756$ (Appendix A). Dividing by $U$ gives the equivalent number of passes of new data. The percentage below is $D'/(U\cdot\text{epochs})$, not a change in loss or accuracy.

| Passes | Effective new-data passes $D'/U$ | Fraction of processed tokens |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 4 | 3.73 | 93% |
| 10 | 7.81 | 78% |
| 40 | 15.17 | 38% |
| 100 | 16.36 | 16% |

The asymptote is $1+R_D^*=16.387756$, approximately 16.4, formerly rounded to “~16” on screen; now retained only in these notes. The original annotation “~40 epochs repeating is worthless” refers to small marginal returns: 40 passes already give 15.17 effective passes, close to the asymptote. It does not mean earlier repetitions had no value. This law is fitted to the authors' conditions, not a universal rule or an instruction to stop every model after four passes.

**Second click: SAME TEXT. LESS NEW LEARNING.** Keep the original figure on the left and replace only the right column. Imagine a corpus of 100 million unique tokens. One pass processes 100M tokens; four passes process 400M but correspond to about 373M fresh tokens under the fitted law; forty passes process 4,000M but correspond to only about 1,517M fresh tokens. These are illustrative rescalings of the fitted effective-data ratio, not separate measured runs with a 100M-token corpus. The unique corpus stays 100M throughout: “equivalent fresh tokens” estimates learning value, not additional text. Early repeats are useful; later repeats cost compute while adding less learning.

**Mathematical detail, speaker notes only.** Start from Chinchilla, $L(N,D)=E+A/N^\alpha+B/D^\beta$: counting all processed tokens as new gives the dashed prediction. The key assumption is that repeats lose the same fraction of value each time. Replace $D$ with effective data $D'$, which grows progressively more slowly and saturates at $U(1+R^*)$. Here $U=U_D=\min\{D_C,D\}$ and $R=R_D=D/U_D-1$ are unique tokens and extra passes. The marginal value of the $(k+1)$-th pass is $R^*(e^{-(k-1)/R^*}-e^{-k/R^*})$: the 2nd pass is 96.82% of new data, the 5th 79.67%, the 11th 53.94%, and the 41st 7.68%, rounded to 97%, 80%, 54%, and 8%. Around $R^*\approx15$ repeats, the marginal value is about $1/e\approx37\%$. The authors call this a “half-life”; mathematically it is an e-folding scale, not the exact time to halve the value.

**How the fit was made.** The coefficients $A,B,E,\alpha,\beta$ are fixed from the authors' C4 fit (Appendix B). They jointly fit only $R_D^*=15.387756$ and the analogous excess-parameter constant $R_N^*=5.309743$, using 182 runs with 7M–9B parameters and 1–500 epochs. They minimize Huber error in log test loss with L-BFGS from a grid of starting points; runs where excess epochs or parameters clearly hurt are excluded as outliers because the law can only improve or plateau. Off-screen, the parameter correction is $N'=U_N+U_N R_N^*(1-e^{-R_N/R_N^*})$, and the full fitted law is $L=E+A/(N')^\alpha+B/(D')^\beta$. The abstract's 400 runs, up to 900B training tokens and 9B parameters, describe the broader experiment set, not the 182-run fit.

**How to read the figure.** Circles are measured runs, tracking the solid fitted curve rather than the dashed new-data prediction; where there are no circles, the curve is an extrapolation of the law. Our reading of the axis labels is 12B unique tokens: 12B processed tokens at one epoch, 48B at four, and 1.2T at 100. The exponential decay is a modeling choice fitted to these data and models, not a universal constant. The limit near 16 is effective new-data passes, not a hard limit on the number of training epochs. Keep the effective-pass table and the cautions above in mind.

**Third click: BETTER DATA — SAME SCORE WITH ~8× FEWER TOKENS.** The other option is to select better data. FineWeb-Edu retains about 8% of FineWeb documents by an educational-value threshold: 15T corpus tokens become 1.3T. Llama-3-70B-Instruct supplies educational-quality annotations; a classifier based on Snowflake-arctic-embed-m learns to predict these scores. The retained documents have a rounded score of at least 3 out of 5. “Top 8%” is shorthand for what this threshold retains, not an exact percentile quota or a universal definition of quality.

FineWeb Figure 11 uses the same 1.71B model and training setup on each dataset. Matrix here is the English Common Crawl section of the Matrix corpus (1.3T tokens; Penedo et al., §3.7), not a different model. Trace the highlighted 33.6% MMLU line: FineWeb-Edu reaches it at 38B processed tokens; Matrix reaches comparable accuracy at about 300B. The approximate marker follows the paper's caption, not a new interpolation of the noisy curve. $300/38=7.8947$, hence ~8× fewer tokens for this score, benchmark and setup.

Corpus sizes are not training tokens: 1.3T is the size of the available FineWeb-Edu dataset, whereas these learning curves show up to 350B tokens actually processed during training. The price of selection is a narrower and smaller pool. The separate FineWeb blog ablation at 350B tokens reports MMLU 33 → 37 and ARC 46 → 57, but HellaSwag 62.7 → 59.7. The blog labels its ablation model 1.82B; the conference paper reports 1.71B for Figure 11. Keep those source contexts distinct. Better MMLU efficiency is not an across-the-board gain.

**Fourth click: synthesis.** The FineWeb plot stays in place and dims slightly. Keep the three statements: scale matters; repetition has diminishing returns; data selection matters. Then make the connection explicit: selection shrinks the pool → a small pool must be repeated when the training budget exceeds its size. Keep this tradeoff in mind: D 13 returns to repeated synthetic data, and D 21 compares rewriting with repetition. Read the question: Given a fixed training budget, which data should we show — and how often? The next slide introduces source pools, a sampler and sampling weights.

**Sources:** [Hoffmann et al., Figure 1, Tables 1, 4 and 6, §4.1, 2022](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2203.15556); [Muennighoff et al., Figure 1 left and Appendix A, NeurIPS 2023, arXiv v5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2305.16264v5#page=1); [Penedo et al., FineWeb, §3.7, §4 and Figure 11, NeurIPS 2024](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/370df50ccfdf8bde18f8f9c2d9151bda-Paper-Datasets_and_Benchmarks_Track.pdf#page=9); [FineWeb blog, FineWeb-Edu ablation at 350B tokens](https://huggingfacefw-blogpost-fineweb-v1.static.hf.space/index.html).
:::

::: {.notes}
Start with the DATA MIXTURES question from D 02: which sources, and how often? The model learns from the material it actually receives. The sampler allocates a limited training budget across domains, so giving one source more tokens takes tokens away from others.

The pools on the left contain web, code, mathematics, knowledge and multimodal data. They stay fixed throughout the scene; the pool silhouettes are schematic, not a quantitative scale. A sampler selects a domain according to its sampling weight, then draws material from that domain. These weights control exposure, not the model's neural-network parameters.

**Start: natural mixture.** The full bar is the fixed token budget, 100%. Segment lengths show how that budget is allocated. “Natural mixture” means sampling in proportion to the available data: Web 60%, Code 15%, Math 5%, Knowledge 12%, Multimodal 8%. These are teaching proportions, not Kimi K3's reported mixture.

**First click: after reweighting.** The second bar has exactly the same total length. Only its shares change: Web 35%, Code 25%, Math 15%, Knowledge 15%, Multimodal 10%. Math rises from 5% to 15%, so it receives three times as much exposure. Its pool has not grown: with repeated sampling, the same material is seen more often. This connects to D 10's diminishing returns from repetition. The factor 3 is relative to the natural-mixture baseline, not a claim of exactly three passes through every example.

Weights are tuned on small models first, then used for the large model. Kimi K3 §3.1 reports domain-specific sampling rates chosen through ablations on smaller models. DoReMi learns domain weights with a small proxy model and transfers them to a larger training run. These sources support the selection procedure; the domain percentages on our diagram remain illustrative. The next click shows a measured result of this weight tuning.

**Second click: does reweighting pay off?** DoReMi compares the same 8B model architecture on The Pile with the same main-training budget: 200k steps, batch size 512, sequence length 1024. The baseline uses The Pile's default domain weights, which already include repeated passes through some sources (typically two, up to three), rather than raw corpus-size proportions. The optimized weights come from a 280M proxy model. “Same budget” refers to the two main 8B runs; tuning the reference and proxy models adds about 8% of one full 8B run's compute (Figure 2 caption).

Read the bars as steps to reach the baseline's final accuracy. The baseline needs 200k steps. Dividing by the reported 2.6× speedup gives 76,923 steps, rounded to 77k; the shorter bar is 1/2.6 = 38.46% of the full bar. The 77k label is our calculation from the rounded speedup, not a step count printed in the paper; §3.2 reports reaching the baseline within 75k steps. At 200k steps, DoReMi is ahead by 6.5 percentage points in average one-shot exact-match accuracy across five tasks. The figure's “6.5% better” denotes percentage points, not a 6.5% relative improvement.

Table 1 shows how strongly the mixture changed: Pile-CC 0.1121 → 0.6057 (about 11% → 61%), ArXiv 0.1052 → 0.0036 (10.5% → 0.4%), PubMed Central 0.1071 → 0.0046 (10.7% → 0.5%), and StackExchange 0.0929 → 0.0153 (9.3% → 1.5%). This mixture nearly switches off those two scientific-text domains and allocates more than half the budget to Pile-CC web text.

The direction is not universal. In Data Mixing Laws (Ye et al., 2024; Figure 8 in v2), a 1B model trained on 100B RedPajama tokens uses the opposite shift: CommonCrawl 67% → 12.5%, ArXiv 4.5% → 25%. The objective is perplexity on The Pile validation set. The optimized mixture reaches the default mixture's result with 0.73 of its training steps. The figure's 1.48× comparison is a scaling-law extrapolation of the default curve, not a measured longer baseline run.

Aioli (Chen et al., 2024) finds that none of the pre-existing methods it evaluates consistently beats uniform sampling across domains on average test perplexity across its tested mixtures. This is a finding within that evaluation, not a claim that reweighting never helps; Aioli itself improves on that baseline. The lesson is that mixtures strongly affect results, but their weights need measurement on small models and checks at the target scale and budget, rather than guesswork.

**Third click: language is another sampling axis.** Return to Common Crawl from D 03. For CC-MAIN-2026-43, the reported language shares are English 42.5647%, Russian 6.3018% and Czech 1.1472%. Restrict to these three languages and divide by their sum, 50.0137%: the corpus shares are 85.1061%, 12.6001% and 2.2938%, displayed as 85.1%, 12.6% and 2.3%.

Let $q_i$ be the corpus share and $p_i$ the training sampling probability. Apply $p_i=q_i^{\alpha}/\sum_j q_j^{\alpha}$, with $\alpha=0.3$, to the unrounded corpus shares. This gives 52.5762%, 29.6424% and 17.7814%, displayed as 52.6%, 29.6% and 17.8%. Both bars sum to 100%. At $\alpha=1$ the mixture follows the data; as $\alpha\to0$, the positive-share languages approach equal sampling probabilities. XLM-R chose 0.3 for its experiments; it is not a universal optimum.

XLM-R v2 §3 states the sampling distribution by reference to Lample and Conneau (2019), with α = 0.3; §5.1 and Figure 5 discuss its tradeoff. The explicit power-normalized formula appears in the cited XLM paper, §3.1, with the letters p and q reversed relative to this slide. Figure 5 is an XLM-100 ablation on Wikipedia, not a measurement of our three-language mixture. The displayed training shares are our calculation using the XLM-R rule on CC 2026 statistics, not the historical XLM-R training recipe.

Common Crawl reports language shares of crawled pages, whereas the XLM sampling rule uses corpus sentence counts. Here the page shares supply the example distribution q; they are not measured token shares. Reading p as an allocation of a fixed token budget assumes equally sized training units. Estimating actual token shares requires tokenizing the data. Recall D 06: less well represented languages can need more tokens for the same text, depending on the tokenizer.

Divide p by q before rounding: English 0.6178, Russian 2.3525, Czech 7.7520. To one decimal these are ×0.6, ×2.4 and ×7.8. Czech gets about 7.8 times its natural-mixture exposure, so with the same fixed pool its material is repeated more. This is a relative exposure multiplier, not an absolute number of epochs. Now compare these sampling choices with Phi-4’s published mixture and its effective passes through each source.

**Sources:** [Kimi K3, §3.1, 2026](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.24653v1#S3.SS1); [DoReMi, 2023, Figure 2, Table 1, §3.1–3.2 and Appendix C](https://arxiv.org/html/2305.10429v4#S1.F2); [The Pile, Table 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2101.00027#S2); [Data Mixing Laws, Figure 8 (v2)](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.16952v2#S4.F8); [Aioli, abstract and §6](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.05735); [XLM-R v2, §3, §5.1 and Figure 5](https://arxiv.org/html/1911.02116v2#S3); [XLM, §3.1 and §3.5, sampling formula](https://arxiv.org/html/1901.07291v1#S3.SS1); [Common Crawl language statistics, CC-MAIN-2026-43](https://commoncrawl.github.io/cc-crawl-statistics/plots/languages).
:::


::: {.notes}
**Introduction — from D 11 to Phi-4.** D 11 showed relative exposure, p/q: Czech received ×7.8 its corpus share, but the absolute training budget was unknown. Phi-4 publishes source sizes and an approximately 10T-token pretraining budget (§3), so we can calculate average passes through each source.

**At opening — corpus.** Table 5 lists Web 1.3T, Web rewrites 290B, Synthetic 290B, Code data 820B, and Acquired sources 580B unique tokens. Their sum is 3,280B = 3.28T, shown as 3.3T. Dividing by this total gives 39.6341%, 8.8415%, 8.8415%, 25.0000%, and 17.6829%. These corpus shares are our calculation; the report does not list them. The integer labels 40 / 9 / 9 / 25 / 18 sum to 101% because they are rounded independently. Segment widths use the unrounded shares and sum to exactly 100%.

**Click 1 — training.** Reveal the second bar and the thin connectors together. The training shares from Table 5 are 15 / 15 / 40 / 20 / 10% of approximately 10T tokens. Web shrinks from about 40% of the corpus to 15% of training, while Synthetic grows from about 9% to 40%. Both full bars mean 100% of their respective totals, not equal absolute token volumes. The sources stay fixed; the allocation of training changes.

**Click 2 — passes through the source.** Passes = training budget × training share ÷ unique source tokens. Synthetic: 10T × 40% ÷ 290B = 4T ÷ 290B ≈ 13.8. Web: 10T × 15% ÷ 1.3T = 1.5T ÷ 1.3T ≈ 1.1538, rounded to 1.2. Table 5 reports 5.2 for Web rewrites, 2.4 for Code data, and 1.7 for Acquired sources; keep these in the notes. Read the takeaway: Phi-4 saw its synthetic data about fourteen times, and its web data about once.

**Connection to D 11.** For Synthetic, p/q = 0.40 / (290 / 3280) ≈ 4.5241, about 4.5. Multiply by the overall budget-to-corpus ratio, 10T / 3.28T ≈ 3.0488: 4.5241 × 3.0488 ≈ 13.7931 passes. The relative multiplier and the absolute number of passes are different quantities.

**Caveats.** The token counts, training budget, and epoch values in the report are rounded. Web rewrites and Synthetic are separate categories in Table 5: do not merge them or assign 40% to their combined total. A pass means average exposure to a source, not a promise to show every document an integer number of times. Synthetic data here means text generated by LLMs; how it is generated and checked comes later.

**Bridge to D 13.** This is the recipe for a particular run; the recipe alone does not prove that this share is better. Next comes the authors' experiment comparing four and twelve passes through a fixed synthetic source at a fixed total token budget. The 13.8 here describes Table 5's final mixture; twelve is a separate experimental setting in Figure 2.

**Source:** [Phi-4 Technical Report, §3 (approximately 10T budget), §3.2, Table 5, 2024](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2412.08905#page=10).
:::

## More unique data is not always better {#frontier-f14-experiment .fv-slide .fv-detail background-color="#ffffff"}

```{=html}
<div class="fv-meta"><span class="fv-id">D 13 / 42</span><span class="fv-cluster">Architecture</span><span class="fv-cluster active">Data</span><span class="fv-cluster">Training</span><span class="fv-cluster">Inference</span><span class="fv-cluster">Tools</span></div>
<div class="fv-body dc-body">
  <div class="dc-kicker"><b>Phi-4 · repeating synthetic data</b><span>Experiment · Figure 2</span></div>
  <div class="dc-evidence">
    <figure class="dc-figure"><img src="assets/data_cases_20261007/phi4_figure2.png" alt="Phi-4 Figure 2: MMLU for 7B and 14B models with 4 and 12 passes through synthetic data"><figcaption>Original Figure 2. Dashed lines: 14B; solid lines: 7B.<br>MMLU tests knowledge across subjects; higher is better.</figcaption></figure>
    <div class="dc-aside">
      <div class="dc-metric"><b class="dc-number">4 / 12</b><span>passes through<br>synthetic data</span></div>
      <p><b>The token budget is fixed</b> within each 4/12 pair. Four passes leave more room for unique web text.</p>
      <p class="dc-highlight">Twelve passes achieve higher MMLU at both model sizes.</p>
      <small>A result for this mixture and these models. It says nothing about the quality of arbitrary synthetic data.</small>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>
<div class="fv-takeaway">In this experiment, repeating high-quality synthetic data helps more than adding unique web text.</div>
<div class="fv-source"><a href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2412.08905#page=9">Phi-4 Technical Report, §3.1, Figure 2</a> · Original plot, not redrawn</div>
```

::: {.notes}
The previous slide showed the mixture used for the main training run. Now we examine the separate experiment in Figure 2: phase-two training of 7B and 14B models from phase-one checkpoints. The authors fix the set of unique synthetic data and compare four and twelve passes through it, keeping the same total token budget within each pair of models of the same size. In the four-pass variant, more unique web text fills the remaining share.

First, read the legend. Dashed lines represent 14B models; solid lines represent 7B models. Each pair compares the number of passes. MMLU tests answers across different academic subjects; the plot uses a 5-shot setting, where the model receives five examples before the question. The vertical axis is MMLU; the horizontal axis is labeled checkpoint/idx and should not be called the number of unique tokens. At both model sizes, the twelve-pass variant achieves a better result.

This supports a limited but useful conclusion: with this budget and data preparation, increasing diversity through web data was less useful than repeating the synthetic source. We are not saying that any synthetic data should be repeated twelve times. The properties of the source and the sampling policy work together here.

The 13.8 in Table 5 and the twelve in Figure 2 refer to different things: the first describes the final mixture; the second is a setting in an experimental comparison. Once we have chosen how often to present a source, the next question is how the team decides which text deserves a place in the mixture.

**Source:** [Phi-4 Technical Report, §3.1, Figure 2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2412.08905#page=9). The slide uses the original plot; no exact numerical differences are claimed from it.
:::

```{=html}
<div class="fv-source"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.11794">DCLM, 2024, Figure 4 (original)</a> · <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.08758">Dodge et al., 2021 (C4 audit)</a></div>
```

::: {.notes}
**Opening.** On D 03, 240T tokens became about 4T. Figure 4 here gives the more precise 3.8T figure, and we can see where the rest went. DCLM-Pool was freshly extracted from Common Crawl HTML with resiliparse: 200B documents and 240T GPT-NeoX tokens. Every percentage in the funnel is a share of the original number of documents, not tokens. By token count, 3.8 / 240 is about 1.6%; documents have different lengths.

**Click 1 — heuristic cleaning.** These heuristics reproduce RefinedWeb. The largest cut is language: half of the documents are not English, connecting back to the Common Crawl languages on D 03 and the language choice on D 11. URL filtering removes 0.8%, the English filter 50.8%, other rules 9.0%, page length 7.9%, repetition 9.6%, and the word-removal ratio 2.0%. These remove 80.1% of the original documents in total, leaving 19.9%. The smaller rules concern length, repeated content, and how much text was stripped out as bad lines.

**Click 2 — deduplication.** Bloom-filter deduplication removes another 6.2% of the original documents, leaving 13.7%. We will work through near-duplicate detection two slides from here.

**Click 3 — quality classifier.** A fastText classifier keeps approximately the top 10% by its score. This removes another 12.3% of the original documents and leaves 1.4%: DCLM-Baseline, with 3.8T tokens. The rounded Figure 4 values give 1.4 / 13.7 ≈ 10.2%, consistent with the top-10% threshold in §4.4.

A quality score guides selection; it does not establish that a text is true. A rare, useful document, such as one containing unusual formulas, may also look suspicious to the scorer. Who decides what counts as the top 10% is the question for the next slide.

**Click 4 — errors in both directions.** This is a separate audit of C4 by Dodge et al. (2021), not an error-rate estimate for DCLM. Blocklist filtering disproportionately removed text from and about minority individuals. Yet machine-translated text and evaluation examples from other NLP benchmarks remained in the corpus.

Contamination is a separate issue: evaluation material has entered the training data. Even high-quality text then compromises the independence of evaluation. Removing duplicates only within the training pool does not resolve this problem by itself.

Provenance records each document's origin and the transformations applied to it. This log lets us investigate both kinds of filtering error afterwards; [W3C PROV](https://www.w3.org/TR/prov-overview/) provides a framework for describing it.

**Caveat and bridge.** Different pipelines may order these stages differently. First, we will examine how Llama 3 trains a quality scorer; then we will return to removing near duplicates.

**Sources:** [DCLM, 2024, Figure 4 and §4.4](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.11794), [Dodge et al., 2021, C4 audit](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.08758), [W3C PROV, 2013](https://www.w3.org/TR/prov-overview/).
:::
