
::: {.notes}
**On opening — how Llama 3 makes a quality score.** Let us make the idea of a quality score concrete by examining one Llama 3 filter. The team collects cleaned web documents, specifies quality requirements, and asks the Llama 2 chat model whether each document meets them. These labels are used to train the compact DistilRoBERTa model, which then scores the large corpus.

There are two distinct roles. Llama 2 helps create the training labels, while the small classifier makes processing at scale computationally affordable. Its score reflects the chosen requirements and the annotator's decisions. It is not a universal measure of truth.

The same section describes separate pipelines for code and mathematics, with different target criteria, HTML processing, and heuristics. Even within one team, there is no single universal filter for every document type. Llama 3 publishes no separate gain for this pipeline.

**First click — what counts as “good”.** Even within the Llama 3 team, quality has different operational definitions. One fastText classifier predicts whether Wikipedia would cite the page; another classifier learns written quality criteria from Llama 2's judgments.

For DCLM, “good” means resembling good answers. Its bigram fastText classifier uses OpenHermes-2.5 instruction data, mostly synthetic, plus ELI5 posts paired with their top answer as positives. Negatives are random documents from DCLM's own RefinedWeb reproduction. It retains the top 10% by score. This is the last funnel step on D 14: these examples define what “top” means.

**Second click — measure the model trained on the selected data.** Table 4 compares filters at the same 1B-1x scale. Core averages centered accuracy over 22 tasks: each task is rescaled so 0 is random guessing and 1 is perfect accuracy, then reported as a percentage. Thus 30.2 on this chart means 0.302 centered accuracy. The chart deliberately starts at 25%, with that truncated axis stated explicitly.

fastText reaches 30.2 Core, compared with 26.1–29.2 for the other model-based methods. The RefinedWeb reproduction without an added model filter scores 27.5; it still includes heuristic filtering and deduplication. Several sophisticated choices do worse than this baseline: PageRank 26.1, SemDedup 27.1, and the classifier on BGE features 27.2. AskLLM scores 28.6, perplexity filtering 29.0, and top-k average logits 29.2. fastText adds 2.7 Core points over no model filter and 1.6 over AskLLM.

Appendix N tests agreement with people: 16 annotators assess roughly 500 documents, with three ratings per document and 71% average inter-annotator agreement. AskLLM agrees with the majority human labels best, at about 82% ROC-AUC, while the fastText classifiers score about 73%. Yet AskLLM produces worse training data: about 28.5 Core versus more than 31 for several fastText classifiers. These are separate Appendix N runs, with similar filtering ratios retaining roughly 15%; they must not replace the Table 4 values on the chart. ROC-AUC measures agreement with human labels, not the downstream Core score.

Human intuition is a weak guide to which documents help a model learn. People choose criteria, examples, and labels, but the useful test of training-data quality is the resulting model's performance. In Table 12, the step from RedPajama to DCLM-baseline adds 4.5 points (30.2 − 25.7); the classifier is its main, though not only, ingredient. This answers the first part of the cover riddle.

Now we return to the next operation in the general diagram: removing duplicates. First, we will calculate similarity between two short strings, then examine Llama 3's actual deduplication levels.

**Sources:** [The Llama 3 Herd of Models, v3, §3.1.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.21783v3#S3.SS1.SSS1); [DataComp-LM, v4, §3.5, §4.4, Tables 4 and 12, Appendix N](https://arxiv.org/html/2406.11794v4).
:::

## Near-duplicates: how similar is similar enough? {#frontier-f15-detail .fv-slide .fv-detail background-color="#ffffff"}

```{=html}
<div class="fv-meta"><span class="fv-id">D 16 / 42</span><span class="fv-cluster">Architecture</span><span class="fv-cluster active">Data</span><span class="fv-cluster">Training</span><span class="fv-cluster">Inference</span><span class="fv-cluster">Tools</span></div>
<div class="fv-body d15-body">
  <div class="d15-motivation">
    <div class="d15-repeat"><strong>60,000×</strong><span>one 61-word sentence, repeated in C4</span></div>
    <div class="d15-evidence">
      <p><b>&gt;1%</b> of unprompted model output is copied verbatim from training data</p>
      <p>after deduplication: memorized text emitted <b>10× less often</b></p>
    </div>
  </div>
  <div class="d15-example fragment" data-fragment-index="1">
    <div class="d15-doc">
      <p class="d15-sentence"><b>A:</b> the drug is safe for children</p>
      <div class="d15-shingles" role="group" aria-label="A: five unique shingles; four shared with B">
        <span class="fv-chip d15-shared">the drug</span><span class="fv-chip d15-shared">drug is</span><span class="fv-chip d15-unique">is safe</span><span class="fv-chip d15-shared">safe for</span><span class="fv-chip d15-shared">for children</span>
      </div>
    </div>
    <div class="d15-doc d15-doc-b">
      <p class="d15-sentence"><b>B:</b> the drug is <span class="fragment fv-highlight d15-negation" data-fragment-index="2">not</span> safe for children</p>
      <div class="d15-shingles" role="group" aria-label="B: six unique shingles; four shared with A">
        <span class="fv-chip d15-shared">the drug</span><span class="fv-chip d15-shared">drug is</span><span class="fv-chip d15-unique">is not</span><span class="fv-chip d15-unique">not safe</span><span class="fv-chip d15-shared">safe for</span><span class="fv-chip d15-shared">for children</span>
      </div>
      <p class="d15-caveat fragment" data-fragment-index="2">opposite meaning — still a "near-duplicate"</p>
    </div>
    <div class="d15-jaccard"><span class="math inline">\(J=\frac{|S(A)\cap S(B)|}{|S(A)\cup S(B)|}=\frac{4}{7}\approx 0.57\)</span></div>
    <div class="d15-decision">≥ 0.5 (example threshold) → near-duplicate: <b>keep A, drop B</b></div>
    <p class="d15-definition">shingle = pair of adjacent words; S = set of unique shingles</p>
  </div>
</div>
<div class="fv-takeaway">Near-dedup applies a similarity threshold; it does not prove equivalent meaning.</div>
<div class="fv-source"><a href="https://doi.org/10.1109/SEQUEN.1997.666900">Broder, 1997</a> · <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.06499">Lee et al., 2022</a> · Teaching example</div>
```

::: {.notes}
**On opening — why remove near-duplicates?** Lee et al. report that one 61-word English sentence occurs more than 60,000 times in C4. Over 1% of the unprompted output of the models studied is copied verbatim from their training data. After deduplication, models emit memorized text ten times less often and reach the same or better accuracy in fewer training steps. These are findings from the study, not universal rates for every language model.

Another finding: train–test overlap affects more than 4% of the validation sets of standard datasets. This is the contamination discussed on D 14.

**Click 1 — how do we find near copies?** Exact string comparison says that “the drug is safe for children” and “the drug is not safe for children” differ. To find near copies, we need a similarity measure. Split each sentence into pairs of adjacent words, ignoring case and punctuation. S(A) and S(B) are sets of unique shingles: repeating a pair within a document does not increase the set size.

A has five pairs and B has six. Four pairs are shared: “the drug”, “drug is”, “safe for”, and “for children”. The union contains 5 + 6 − 4 = 7 distinct pairs. Jaccard similarity is therefore J = 4/7 ≈ 0.57. At the teaching threshold of 0.5, the pair is considered a near-duplicate: keep A and drop B. This threshold is an illustration, not a recommended setting; keeping A is also just the example's selection decision.

**Click 2 — what is the catch?** The single word “not” reverses the meaning, while most word pairs remain shared. Changing an important number can have the same effect. A threshold is therefore an engineering decision that can be wrong, not proof of equivalent meaning.

**Scale.** Comparing all pairs among 200 billion documents in DCLM-Pool would require N(N − 1)/2 ≈ 2 × 10²² comparisons. Exact all-pairs comparison is computationally infeasible at this scale. In practice, MinHash sketches approximate Jaccard similarity; combined with locality-sensitive hashing, they find candidate near-duplicates without enumerating every pair. Store text normalization, shingle size, and the threshold together with the rule version.

**Provenance.** Log the rule, computed similarity, retained document and dropped document so that the selection reason can be reconstructed and the rule reconsidered. The log preserves the link from B to the retained A; see [W3C PROV](https://www.w3.org/TR/prov-overview/) for the provenance framework.

**Bridge.** Next, we will examine the deduplication levels and rules described in Llama 3.

**Sources:** [Broder, 1997](https://doi.org/10.1109/SEQUEN.1997.666900), [Lee et al., 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.06499), [W3C PROV](https://www.w3.org/TR/prov-overview/).
:::

## Deduplication can remove the better data {#frontier-f15-case-dedup .fv-slide .fv-detail background-color="#ffffff"}

```{=html}
<div class="fv-meta"><span class="fv-id">D 17 / 42</span><span class="fv-cluster">Architecture</span><span class="fv-cluster active">Data</span><span class="fv-cluster">Training</span><span class="fv-cluster">Inference</span><span class="fv-cluster">Tools</span></div>
<div class="fv-body dc-body">
  <div class="d17-llama">
    <div class="d17-chain"><b class="fv-label">Llama 3</b><div><b>URL</b><span>latest version</span></div><span class="fv-arrow" aria-hidden="true">→</span><div><b>document</b><span>global MinHash</span></div><span class="fv-arrow" aria-hidden="true">→</span><div><b>line</b><span>lines seen &gt; 6× per 30M docs</span></div></div>
    <p class="d17-paradox">Line dedup removes menus and cookie banners — and some frequent high-quality text. <b>Evaluations still improved.</b></p>
  </div>
  <div class="d17-fineweb fragment" data-fragment-index="1">
    <div class="dc-kicker"><b>FineWeb · crawl 2013-48</b><span>Global dedup across 96 crawls, applied to one old crawl</span></div>
    <div class="d17-bar-row"><p><b>kept · ~10% · 31B tokens</b><span>more ads, badly formatted text</span></p><div class="d17-track"><div class="d17-bar d17-kept" style="width:10%" aria-hidden="true"></div></div></div>
    <div class="d17-bar-row d17-winner"><p><b>removed · ~90% · 171B tokens <small>after its own dedup</small></b><span><strong>trained a better model</strong> ↗</span></p><div class="d17-track"><div class="d17-bar fv-accent" style="width:90%" aria-hidden="true"></div></div></div>
    <p class="d17-scale fv-muted">Bar length = share of the original crawl · token counts reflect the stated dedup steps.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="d17-why fragment" data-fragment-index="2">
    <div class="fv-label">Why? · Authors’ hypothesis</div>
    <p>Huge clusters (100,000s of copies in every crawl) → removing them helps.</p>
    <p>A page with no copy in any other crawl is often worse.</p>
    <p class="d17-result"><b>Dedup each crawl separately: 20T tokens, matches RefinedWeb</b> · Dedup globally: 4T tokens, ≈ no dedup.</p>
  </div>
</div>
<div class="fv-takeaway">Judge a filter by its effect on training; it may also remove good text.</div>
<div class="fv-source"><a href="https://arxiv.org/html/2407.21783v3#S3.SS1.SSS1">The Llama 3 Herd of Models, §3.1.1 — De-duplication</a> · <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.17557">FineWeb, 2024, §3 deduplication ablations</a></div>
```

::: {.notes}
**On opening — Llama 3.** URL deduplication keeps the latest version of each page; document deduplication uses global MinHash; line deduplication removes lines seen more than six times within each bucket of 30 million documents. “More than six” is not “six or more”, and the count is within each bucket, not across the whole corpus. These are different rules. The illustrative Jaccard threshold of 0.5 on D16 is not part of this recipe.

Manual inspection found that line dedup removes menus and cookie banners, but also frequent high-quality text. Evaluations still improved: the overall distribution can improve even when some good text is lost. The authors give no numerical gain isolated to this threshold.

**Click 1 — FineWeb, crawl 2013-48.** Global MinHash across 96 crawls retained only about 10% of this old crawl; about 90% was removed as duplicate data when processing the crawls from newest to oldest. The authors trained separately on the retained 31B tokens and on the removed data, which yielded 171B tokens after its own within-crawl deduplication. The latter trained a better model. Inspection found more ads, incoherent keyword lists and badly formatted text in the retained data.

The bars encode the paper's approximate original 10% / 90% split, not the ratio 31 / (31 + 171). The token counts describe different processing stages: the removed portion was deduplicated again. The paper also reports about 460B tokens before this additional deduplication; its rounded 10% / 90% statement is not an exact token-ratio calculation.

**Click 2 — the authors' hypothesis.** Deduplication helps mainly by removing giant clusters of hundreds of thousands of copies present in every crawl. Further deduplication of small clusters, with fewer than about 100 copies (roughly the number of crawls), can hurt. A page repeated across many crawls may simply be useful material kept online for a long time; repetition alone is not evidence of poor quality. Data with no copy in any other crawl may be worse or further from the target distribution. Treat this as an explanation consistent with the experiment, not a proven rule for every page.

Deduplicating each crawl separately produced 20T tokens; training on a random sample from all crawls matched RefinedWeb. Global dedup produced 4T tokens and little improvement over no dedup. These are corpus sizes, not matched training budgets. Targeted quality filtering may suit the long tail better than more deduplication.

**If exact scores are needed.** Consult and re-check the plots in the [FineWeb blog](https://huggingface.co/spaces/HuggingFaceFW/blogpost-fineweb-v1) before quoting them orally; the numerical plot readings are intentionally omitted here.

**Bridge.** We now move from cleaning existing records to creating new candidates: first generation and verification, then knowledge rephrasing.

**Sources:** [The Llama 3 Herd of Models, §3.1.1 — De-duplication](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.21783v3#S3.SS1.SSS1); [FineWeb, 2024, §3.4](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.17557).
:::

::: {.notes}
On opening, D 14 shows that DCLM retains ~1.4% of documents; this is not the token retention fraction. On click 1, D 15 separates human agreement from training value: AskLLM's ~82% ROC-AUC against human labels does not beat fastText downstream. On click 2, connect D 16's near-duplicate threshold to D 17's FineWeb case: the removed ~90% of crawl 2013-48 trained a better model than the retained ~10%, and removing huge duplicate clusters is the authors' explanatory hypothesis. On click 3, “Every filter is a hypothesis; training results are the test” answers D 02's “What should we keep?” The decision is justified by training outcomes, not by a filter's name. <div class="fv-meta"><span class="fv-id">D 18 / 42</span><span class="fv-cluster">Architecture</span><span class="fv-cluster active">Data</span><span class="fv-cluster">Training</span><span class="fv-cluster">Inference</span><span class="fv-cluster">Tools</span></div>

```{=html}
<div class="fv-source"><a href="https://arxiv.org/html/2410.24198">SelfCodeAlign, 2024, Table 9</a> · <a href="https://arxiv.org/html/2607.24653v1#S3.SS1">Kimi K3, §3.1, 2026</a> · <a href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2412.08905#page=10">Phi-4, Table 5</a></div>
```

::: {.notes}
**On opening — why generate, and why verify?** In Phi-4, the Synthetic category accounts for 40% of pretraining tokens (Table 5; D 12). This is the named category, not the sum of every synthetic source: web rewrites are listed separately. Where do these data come from, and why trust them? When the examples we need are scarce, we generate candidates. But fluent text does not automatically make good training data.

Read the chain: a basis (source material or a specification with facts and constraints) → generator → many candidates → verifier → kept examples. Verification is a separate role in the process; it does not necessarily require a different model. Different data require different checks: run code against tests; compare rephrased knowledge with its source, as Kimi K3 does; use a judge model to assess style and suitability. There is no need to apply all three mechanically. Kimi K3 §3.1 describes source-fidelity checks for rephrased knowledge and mathematics, but reports no acceptance or rejection rate.

**Click 1 — how much survives?** SelfCodeAlign uses the base CodeQwen1.5-7B model to derive tasks from code and generate solutions together with their tests. Without filtering, only about 24% of the selected solutions pass their own tests: Table 9 reports 24.1% for all 27.7k randomly selected examples and 24.2% for the matched 15.6k subset. The display rounds this to 24%; 6 / 25 = 0.24. Roughly three quarters fail the generated tests despite being plausible candidates. A failing solution–test pair is not useful evidence of correct code; the generated tests themselves can also be wrong.

Pipeline detail if asked: 250k Python functions with docstrings are selected from 5M in The Stack V1. The base model extracts concepts, writes a task, and samples multiple solution–test pairs. Sandbox execution rejects failing pairs; one passing solution per task is selected at random. The final training dataset contains 74k pairs. Table 9 is a component analysis based on 37k seeds, not the final 74k-example run; its ~24% is the execution pass rate among responses selected without filtering, not the final pipeline yield.

**Click 2 — matched-size evidence.** At the same 15.6k examples, failures only scores 57.9, random unchecked scores 61.6, and passes only scores 65.2 on HumanEval+ pass@1. Execution-based selection adds 3.6 percentage points over random selection; failures only loses 3.7 points versus random and 7.3 versus passes only. The chart deliberately uses a 50–70% axis, labelled as starting at 50. Learning from failing solutions hurts relative to the other selection strategies; this comparison does not establish degradation relative to the untrained base model.

Additional result, from Table 1: the final SelfCodeAlign-CQ-7B trained on 74k verified examples reaches 67.1 on HumanEval+, compared with 65.2 for CodeLlama-70B-Instruct (a 1.9-point difference). Keep this full-run result distinct from the 65.2 in the component analysis.

**Limits of verification.** A judge can make mistakes, and tests cover only selected cases. Passing self-generated tests is evidence, not proof of correctness. Generation expands the candidate set; verification determines what enters training.

**Bridge.** Next, a teaching example shows how one additional test changes the selection decision.

**Sources:** [SelfCodeAlign, 2024, §2, §4 and Tables 1, 9](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.24198); [Kimi K3, §3.1, 2026](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.24653v1#S3.SS1); [Phi-4, Table 5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2412.08905#page=10).
:::

## Synthetic code: a counterexample changes the selection {#frontier-f16-detail .fv-slide .fv-detail background-color="#ffffff"}

```{=html}
<div class="fv-meta"><span class="fv-id">D 19 / 42</span><span class="fv-cluster">Architecture</span><span class="fv-cluster active">Data</span><span class="fv-cluster">Training</span><span class="fv-cluster">Inference</span><span class="fv-cluster">Tools</span></div>
<div class="fv-body d16-body">
  <div class="d16-spec"><b>Specification:</b> return the sum of all even integers in xs, including negative values.</div>
  <div class="d16-candidates"><div><b>Generated A</b><pre><code>sum(x for x in xs
    if x &gt; 0 and x % 2 == 0)</code></pre></div><div><b>Generated B</b><pre><code>sum(x for x in xs
    if x % 2 == 0)</code></pre></div></div>
  <table class="d16-tests"><thead><tr><th scope="col">Test input: xs</th><th scope="col">Expected</th><th scope="col">Result A</th><th scope="col">Result B</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td><code>[2, 4]</code></td><td>6</td><td>6</td><td>6</td></tr><tr class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1"><td><code>[-2, 0, 4]</code></td><td><b>2</b></td><td class="d16-fail">4 ≠ 2</td><td class="d16-pass">2</td></tr></tbody></table>
  <div class="d16-selection fragment" data-fragment-index="1"><b>Selected: B</b><span>passed the tests shown — not a proof</span></div>
  <div class="d16-reality fv-grid2 fragment" data-fragment-index="2">
    <div class="d16-blind-spots"><p>Same model writes the code and the tests<br><b>→ shared blind spots</b></p><small>as in SelfCodeAlign (D 18)</small></div>
    <div class="d16-evalplus"><div class="d16-evalplus-heading"><span class="fv-label">EvalPlus</span><strong class="fv-big">×80 tests</strong></div><p>HumanEval → HumanEval+: pass@k drops by up to 19–29%, model rankings change</p></div>
  </div>
</div>
<div class="fv-takeaway">A verifier must test the requirements: one convenient test can admit a wrong solution.</div>
<div class="fv-source"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.24198">SelfCodeAlign, 2024 — execution-based selection</a> · <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.01210">EvalPlus, 2023</a> · Author-created example; results computed in Python</div>
```

::: {.notes}
**On opening — what does passing mean?** Start with the specification: the function must return the sum of all even integers in the input list, including negative values. The list on the slide is called xs. The variable x refers to each number in turn. The check x % 2 == 0 selects values whose remainder after division by two is zero: even integers.

Candidate A adds another condition: x must be greater than zero. The specification does not require this. Candidate B keeps only the evenness check. Given [2, 4], both return 6. If our test set contains only this convenient example, the incorrect solution passes selection.

The table contains results from executing Python, not judgments made by a language model. These A and B belong to a separate teaching example; they are not linked to variants or outcomes on D 18.

**Click 1 — a counterexample changes the selection.** Now supply [-2, 0, 4]. All three numbers are even, and their sum is 2. A discards −2 and returns 4. B returns 2. Executing the code exposes a specific violation of the specification. The negative value −2 distinguishes the candidates: excluding zero does not change the sum.

Select B, with a narrow conclusion: it passed the two tests shown. A finite test set does not prove correctness for every valid input. Mention the empty list [] orally: both expressions return 0. It is another valid case, but it does not distinguish these candidates, so it is omitted from the table.

**Click 2 — shared blind spots and stronger tests.** On D 18, SelfCodeAlign showed that execution-based selection helps. However, the same base model generates both the solutions and their tests. If it overlooks negative numbers when writing the solution, it may overlook them in the tests too. This shared-blind-spot scenario is the teaching example's inference, not a measured error rate from SelfCodeAlign. The tests themselves must therefore be checked against the specification.

EvalPlus (Liu et al., 2023) expanded HumanEval's tests by 80× to create HumanEval+. Across 26 models, the authors report pass@k reductions of up to 19.3–28.9% (rounded to 19–29% on the slide). Previously accepted programs were exposed as incorrect, and model rankings changed: WizardCoder-CodeLlama and Phind-CodeLlama outperformed ChatGPT on HumanEval+, but not on HumanEval. This is why the stronger HumanEval+ metric used on D 18 was introduced.

**Bridge.** Here, the verifier checked an executable result. For rephrased knowledge, the question is different: does the new text preserve the meaning of the source? Next, Kimi K2.

**Sources:** [SelfCodeAlign, 2024 — execution-based selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.24198); [EvalPlus, 2023, abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.01210). Author-created example; results computed in Python.
:::

## One source of knowledge, several training representations {#frontier-f16-case .fv-slide background-color="#ffffff"}

```{=html}
<div class="fv-meta"><span class="fv-id">D 20 / 42</span><span class="fv-cluster">Architecture</span><span class="fv-cluster active">Data</span><span class="fv-cluster">Training</span><span class="fv-cluster">Inference</span><span class="fv-cluster">Tools</span></div>
<div class="fv-body dc-body d20-body">
  <p class="d20-bridge">D 10: repeating the same text loses value. Rephrasing repeats the knowledge, not the text.</p>
  <div class="dc-evidence">
    <figure class="dc-figure"><img src="assets/data_cases_20261007/kimi_k2_figure4.svg" alt="Original Kimi K2 Figure 4: a long document is split into chunks, rewritten sequentially using previous chunks as context, and concatenated into a full passage."><figcaption>Kimi K2, Figure 4: long documents are rewritten chunk by chunk, with previous chunks as context.</figcaption></figure>
    <div class="d20-example">
      <div class="fv-panel d20-source">
        <div class="d20-card-heading"><b>Source</b></div>
        <p>At sea level water boils at 100 °C; on Everest at about 70 °C, because air pressure is lower.</p>
      </div>
      <div class="d20-variants fragment" data-fragment-index="1">
        <div class="fv-panel">
          <div class="d20-card-heading"><b>Textbook</b><span>✓ faithful</span></div>
          <p>Boiling point falls with pressure: 100 °C at sea level, ≈70 °C on Everest.</p>
        </div>
        <div class="fv-panel">
          <div class="d20-card-heading"><b>Q&amp;A</b><span>✓ faithful</span></div>
          <p>Why below 100 °C on Everest? Lower air pressure → ≈70 °C.</p>
        </div>
        <div class="fv-panel">
          <div class="d20-card-heading"><b>Learning note</b><span>✓ faithful</span></div>
          <p>pressure ↓ → boiling point ↓ · 100 °C → ≈70 °C</p>
        </div>
      </div>
      <div class="d20-check fragment" data-fragment-index="2">
        <div class="fv-panel d20-rejected">
          <p>On Everest water boils at ≈70 °C <strong class="fv-accent d20-cause">because it is colder there.</strong></p>
          <div class="d20-verdict">✗ rejected — fidelity check: cause changed</div>
        </div>
        <p class="d20-check-note">Each rephrasing is compared with its source before it enters training.</p>
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>
<div class="fv-takeaway">Rewriting aims to preserve the knowledge while changing how it is presented.</div>
<div class="fv-source"><a href="https://arxiv.org/html/2507.20534#S2.SS2">Kimi K2: Open Agentic Intelligence, §2.2, Figure 4, 2025</a> · Original figure; right: teaching example</div>
```

::: {.notes}
**On opening.** In the previous example, the verifier checked a program by executing it. That check is usually not applicable to factual text: we need to check fidelity to the source. Recall D 10: repeating the same text becomes less useful. Rephrasing gives us a new text with the same knowledge.

Read Figure 4 from left to right. A long document cannot reliably be rewritten in one go because of output-length limits. It is split into chunks, rewritten sequentially with previously rewritten chunks as context, and stitched back together into a complete passage. This preserves continuity across the document.

The source on the right is our teaching example, not an excerpt from Kimi K2. At standard sea-level pressure, pure water boils at 100 °C; near Everest's summit, about 70 °C is a rounded estimate. The exact value varies with atmospheric pressure. Lower pressure is the reason for the lower boiling point.

**Click 1.** Inspired by WRAP, Kimi K2 uses prompts that vary style and perspective to diversify the language while preserving facts. The three cards illustrate one piece of knowledge as a textbook passage, a question and answer, and a learning note. These particular cards are our illustration, not styles quoted from the paper. For mathematical data, Kimi K2 specifically rewrites high-quality documents in a learning-note style following SwallowMath, and translates high-quality mathematical materials from other languages into English.

**Click 2.** A rephrasing can sound fluent while changing a fact. The fourth card changes the cause: the lower boiling point is due to lower air pressure, not to colder surroundings. Kimi K2 compares each rephrased passage with its source for semantic alignment before training. This fidelity-verification step is described separately in §2.2; it is not part of the original Figure 4. The illustration makes the check concrete without adding it to the published diagram. This continues D 16, where one “not” changes the meaning, and D 19, where a convenient test misses an error.

The aim is to change the representation of knowledge while preserving the knowledge itself. If rewriting drops a condition or changes a fact, the new text does not automatically become a useful training example. Checking fidelity to the source is therefore part of data preparation.

But a plausible process diagram does not establish a measured effect. The authors ran a separate ablation: they compared repeating the original text, repeating one rewritten version, and presenting ten versions once each. That is our next slide, D 21.

**Sources:** [Kimi K2: Open Agentic Intelligence, §2.2, Figure 4](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.20534#S2.SS2). Fidelity verification is described in the text, not in Figure 4. The water example is author-created; the rounded temperature and pressure explanation are supported by [Royal Meteorological Society, “Boiling Water with Ice”](https://www.metlink.org/experiment/boiling-water-with-ice/).
:::


::: {.notes}
**On opening.** The three rows reproduce the conditions from Kimi K2, Table 1. SimpleQA evaluates short answers to factual questions; the numbers are percentages of correct answers, so higher is better. The source is raw wiki-text. Presenting it ten times yields 23.76.

**Click 1 — one rewrite, ten passes.** Rewriting the source once and presenting that corpus ten times raises the score to 27.39: 27.39 − 23.76 = 3.63 percentage points. A single change of wording already outperforms simple repetition of the source.

**Click 2 — ten rewrites, one pass.** Preparing ten different rewritten versions and presenting each once yields 28.94: 28.94 − 23.76 = 5.18 percentage points above the original. Diversity across several variants adds another gain. These differences are calculated from published values; we did not run a new model evaluation.

The icons show the same knowledge encountered ten times in all three conditions; only its surface form changes. This resolves the tension from D 10 and from Phi-4. What loses value under repetition is the same wording, not the knowledge. Scarce is unique information, not tokens, and repetition is a weight we set deliberately.

**Caveats.** The comparison uses an early K2 checkpoint, not the released model's final score or its full training run. The ten variants belong to the ablation. For large knowledge corpora in the main run, the authors report at most two rewrites. The number of passes alone does not establish an equal token count, because rewritten documents can differ in length.

**Optional addition — BeyondWeb (no slide fragment).** Independent supporting evidence comes from DatologyAI, a company that sells data curation: this is a vendor report. With a Llama-3.2-1B model and 20B training tokens, 20B unique tokens give 46.2, the same 10B seen twice give 45.5, and the mixture with rephrased variants gives 50.4. Repetition costs little; rephrasing wins. These are average accuracies across 14 tasks and 0-shot/5-shot settings, not SimpleQA. The rephrasing condition mixes 10B original tokens with 10B synthetic tokens derived from the same source. Values and setup checked against [BeyondWeb, §4.1 and §4.3](https://www.datologyai.com/blog/beyondweb) on 2026-10-28; check the report before quoting the numbers aloud.

**Bridge.** So far, we have varied how knowledge is presented. Next, we focus on example length and ask what forces the model to connect its distant parts.

**Source:** [Kimi K2, §2.2, Table 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.20534#S2.SS2). Teaching calculations: 27.39 − 23.76 = 3.63; 28.94 − 23.76 = 5.18 percentage points.
:::

## What we know so far {#data-recap-synthetic .fv-slide .data-recap-slide background-color="#ffffff"}

::: {.data-recap data-section="synthetic"}
:::

::: {.notes}
On opening, D 18 reports that only ~24% of unfiltered SelfCodeAlign solutions pass their generated tests (24.1% in Table 9's full random sample), rather than a universal synthetic-data acceptance rate. On click 1, D 19 shows why test coverage matters: HumanEval+ adds 80× tests and exposes pass@k reductions of up to 19.3–28.9%, rounded to 19–29% on the slide. On click 2, D 20–21 distinguish repeating knowledge from repeating wording: Kimi K2's early-checkpoint ablation improves SimpleQA from 23.76 to 28.94 using ten rewrites once instead of the original ten times. On click 3, connect verification to D 02's “What examples should we create?”: generated candidates become useful only when their checks fit the intended learning task. Next, D 22 turns to long-context data and asks how examples teach dependencies between distant passages.
:::

## Long-context data and curriculum {#frontier-f18 .fv-slide background-color="#ffffff"}

```{=html}
<div class="fv-meta"><span class="fv-id">D 22 / 42</span><span class="fv-cluster">Architecture</span><span class="fv-cluster active">Data</span><span class="fv-cluster">Training</span><span class="fv-cluster">Inference</span><span class="fv-cluster">Tools</span></div>
<div class="fv-body f18-body">
  <svg class="f18-document" viewBox="0 0 1488 250" width="1488" height="250" role="img" aria-label="A long document with links between distant passages">
    <text x="0" y="25" font-size="24" fill="#626262">One document — several long-range dependencies</text>
    <rect x="0" y="113" width="353" height="88" fill="#f3f3f3" stroke="#c5c5c5"/>
    <path d="M22 140H326M22 156H300M22 172H320" stroke="#d1d1d1" stroke-width="4"/>
    <g class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1"><rect x="353" y="113" width="1134" height="88" fill="#f3f3f3" stroke="#c5c5c5"/><path d="M380 140H640M380 156H676M380 172H652M726 140H1010M726 156H999M726 172H1030M1100 140H1450M1100 156H1434M1100 172H1455" stroke="#d1d1d1" stroke-width="4"/><text x="1458" y="237" text-anchor="end" font-size="24" fill="#626262">Sequence length →</text></g>
    <g class="fragment" data-fragment-index="2"><path d="M128 113Q330 1 597 113M597 113Q900 -14 1285 113M128 201Q710 271 1285 201" stroke="#141414" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><rect x="59" y="123" width="138" height="67" fill="#bef264" stroke="#141414"/><text x="128" y="163" text-anchor="middle" font-size="26">Premise A</text><rect x="519" y="123" width="156" height="67" fill="#bef264" stroke="#141414"/><text x="597" y="163" text-anchor="middle" font-size="26">Link B</text><rect x="1205" y="123" width="160" height="67" fill="#bef264" stroke="#141414"/><text x="1285" y="163" text-anchor="middle" font-size="26">Result A+B</text></g>
  </svg>
  <div class="f18-curriculum"><div class="fv-label">Kimi K3<br>Training length</div><div><b>8K</b><span>pre-training</span></div><i>→</i><div><b>64K</b><span>pre-training</span></div><i>→</i><div><b>256K</b><span>mid-training</span></div><i>→</i><div class="f18-last"><b>1M</b><span>mid-training</span></div></div>
</div>
<div class="fv-takeaway">A large context window does not guarantee use of distant information.</div>
<div class="fv-source"><a href="https://arxiv.org/html/2607.24653v1#S3.SS4">Kimi K3, §3.4, 2026</a> (the report calls the last two stages “cooldown”) · <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06654">RULER, 2024</a> · Document: teaching schematic</div>
```

::: {.notes}
After the architecture block, it is tempting to say: expand the available window, and the model will handle long documents. But fitting a sequence and using distant information are different requirements. The data must create a task that actually needs that information to be solved.

*First click: reveal the document's length; second click: reveal the links between passages.*

At first, we simply added text. Now we have premise A, a distant link B, and a result that requires both. The arcs represent dependencies in the task, not measured attention weights. A long sequence could consist of independent short tasks and never test this kind of connection.

The middle row shows a curriculum: a sequence of training stages with different lengths. The Kimi K3 report specifies eight thousand, sixty-four thousand, two hundred and fifty-six thousand, and one million tokens.

Keep three factors separate — data dependencies, training length, and architectural state: what the data requires us to connect, what length was used in training, and what the architecture keeps accessible. A large window alone does not guarantee the required quality. It makes a long input possible. We need a separate task to test whether the model uses the connection. Next, we will build such a task with an exact answer and distracting records.

**Optional detail.** The length schedule comes from a specific report; it is not a universal recipe. The report calls the final two stages “cooldown”; other teams call this stage mid-training: a short final phase of pre-training on a selected mixture, with the learning rate annealed to zero. Distances in the diagram are not proportional to token counts. Training length, available context window, and performance on long-range dependencies are separate characteristics.

**Sources:** [Kimi K3, §3.4, 2026](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.24653v1#S3.SS4), [RULER, 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06654).

Positional scaling and longer-sequence training are coordinated in [LongRoPE §3.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.13753), with short-context performance retested separately. Whole songs preserve distant links between choruses, arrangement and ending: [YuE2 §2.4 / §3.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.33757v1) packs songs into 24,576 positions, whereas MERT2-FS uses 30–360-second recordings; sequence positions and duration are different quantities.
:::

## Long context: two facts, distractors, and an exact answer {#frontier-f18-detail .fv-slide .fv-detail background-color="#ffffff"}

```{=html}
<div class="fv-meta"><span class="fv-id">D 23 / 42</span><span class="fv-cluster">Architecture</span><span class="fv-cluster active">Data</span><span class="fv-cluster">Training</span><span class="fv-cluster">Inference</span><span class="fv-cluster">Tools</span></div>
<div class="fv-body d18-body">
  <div class="d18-question"><b>Task:</b> what is the code for project Lyra? Reply with the code only.</div>
  <div class="d18-context"><div class="d18-fact"><small>Early passage</small><code>Lyra → key K7</code></div><div class="d18-noise"><small>Distractors</small><code>Lyra2 → K8 · K8 → 38</code></div><div class="d18-fact"><small>Distant passage</small><code>K7 → code 83</code></div><div class="d18-noise d18-tail"><small>Distractors</small><span>… other records …</span></div></div>
  <div class="d18-reasoning fragment" data-fragment-index="1"><b>Both facts are needed:</b><code>Lyra</code><span>→</span><code>K7</code><span>→</span><code class="d18-answer">83</code><em>Key K8 does not apply.</em></div>
  <div class="d18-protocol fragment" data-fragment-index="2"><div class="d18-curriculum"><b>Curriculum: harder data</b><div><span>2K</span><i>→</i><span>8K</span><i>→</i><span>32K</span></div><p>More distractors; facts placed further apart.<br>The link Lyra → K7 → 83 stays intact.</p></div><div class="d18-eval"><b>Evaluation: vary conditions</b><p>New names and codes · different fact positions · different lengths L</p><span class="math inline">\(\text{Exact match}=\frac{\text{correct codes}}{\text{total tasks}}\)</span></div></div>
  <p class="d18-kimi"><b>Kimi K3 builds 1M-token tasks the same way:</b> “the embedded tasks can be solved only by attending to information scattered across the full 1M-token context.”</p>
</div>
<div class="fv-takeaway">A long-context test must require a distant connection and vary the relevant facts' positions.</div>
<div class="fv-source"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06654">RULER, 2024 — retrieval and variable tracking</a> · Original teaching task; illustrative lengths: 2K/8K/32K · <a href="https://arxiv.org/html/2607.24653v1#S3.SS4">Kimi K3 §3.4</a></div>
```

::: {.notes}
The answer must contain only the code for project Lyra. An early passage states that the project is linked to key K7. A distant passage states that key K7 corresponds to code 83. Neither fact alone provides the complete path from the project name to the code.

Between them are distractors: irrelevant records. There is a similar name, Lyra2, linked to K8, and a mapping from K8 to code 38. These records do not contradict the relevant facts. They create the risk of selecting a similar name or the nearest number instead of following the correct connection.

*First click: reveal the answer chain.*

We start with the exact name Lyra, obtain K7, and then look up the value for that specific key. The answer is 83. Key K8 is not part of this chain.

*Second click: show the curriculum and evaluation.*

In this teaching curriculum, lengths grow from two thousand tokens to eight thousand and then thirty-two thousand. We increase the number of distractors and the distance between the facts. The required connection stays intact. These lengths belong to our example, not to the Kimi K3 schedule.

For evaluation, we vary names and codes, the positions of both facts, and the total context length, denoted by L. Exact match is the fraction of tasks that return the correct code. We define the comparison rule in advance, such as trimming leading and trailing whitespace. We inspect results separately for each length so that an overall average does not hide failures on long inputs.

The slide shows a protocol, not measured model success. This task tests one specific distant connection; it does not cover every kind of reasoning. Now we return to Kimi K3: how can we ensure that long examples appear in the training mix and distribute the required information across those examples?

**Optional detail.** If we always keep the answer 83 or use the same fact positions, a shortcut becomes available without finding the required connection. New names, codes, and positions help test the mechanism itself. This example is inspired by retrieval and variable-tracking tasks, but is not presented as an official RULER test.

**Sources:** [RULER, 2024 — retrieval and variable tracking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06654).

In the Lyra example, a local passage was not enough to obtain the code. Now we can read how the Kimi K3 authors express a similar requirement for a multimodal corpus: embedded tasks should be solvable only by using information spread across the full million-token context. This is a requirement for the design of the training data, not just for sequence length.

To achieve this, the authors reorder and combine multimodal documents and subtasks. The information required for the solution is located in different parts; the Lyra diagram above illustrates the principle, not an official Kimi example or measured attention result.

Why does this operation matter? If each subtask can be solved entirely from a small nearby passage, the model can rely on local processing even within a long input. Distributed dependencies make distant information necessary.

This is the team's stated recipe. Section 3.4 does not quantify the individual contribution of reordering and combining, so we should not present this slide as evidence of a specific quality gain. Next we examine how much of the training mix should contain long data, before moving from documents to interaction trajectories.

**Source:** [Kimi K3, §3.4, Long-Context Data](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.24653#S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2).
:::

## Long examples need a place in the training mix {#frontier-f18-case-sampling .fv-slide background-color="#ffffff"}

```{=html}
<div class="fv-meta"><span class="fv-id">D 24 / 42</span><span class="fv-cluster">Architecture</span><span class="fv-cluster active">Data</span><span class="fv-cluster">Training</span><span class="fv-cluster">Inference</span><span class="fv-cluster">Tools</span></div>
<div class="fv-body dc-body">
  <p class="d24-sampling"><b>Kimi K3 §3.4:</b> Long, coherent documents and videos are sampled more often so that short sequences do not crowd them out.</p>
  <figure class="d24-prolong"><img src="assets/data_long_context_20261028/prolong-figure3.svg" alt="ProLong Figure 3: long-context data share from 20% to 100%. Average long-task performance after SFT peaks at 60% and falls at 100%; short-task performance declines as the long-data share grows. Blue is before SFT and orange is after SFT." /><figcaption>ProLong · original Figure 3 · fixed 5B-token training budget</figcaption></figure>
  <div class="d24-findings"><p><b>60% long + 40% short</b>works best</p><p><b>100% long data</b>hurts long-context results</p></div>
</div>
<div class="fv-takeaway">Long data needs a share of the mix, not all of it.</div>
<div class="fv-source"><a href="https://arxiv.org/html/2607.24653v1#S3.SS4">Kimi K3 §3.4</a> · <a href="https://arxiv.org/html/2410.02660v1#S3.F3">Gao et al., How to Train Long-Context Language Models (Effectively), 2024 · §3.2 / Figure 3; §2.1 / Figure 1</a></div>
```

::: {.notes}
Kimi K3 upsamples long, coherent documents and videos so that short sequences do not dominate the long-context distribution. The 8K → 64K → 256K → 1M schedule is already shown on D 22; those stage lengths describe a curriculum, not the share of long examples in a mixture. Source: [Kimi K3 §3.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.24653v1#S3.SS4).

ProLong tests the mixture directly at a fixed budget of 5B tokens, using books and code repositories as long data and ShortMix as short data. The original Figure 3 compares several long tasks, their average, and short-task performance. The best average is obtained with 60% long and 40% short data (§3.2); short-task performance declines as the long share increases. Evaluating after SFT matters: the orange long-task average falls sharply at 100%, even though some individual tasks benefit from more long data. This is a measured recipe for these experiments, not a universal 60/40 optimum. [Gao et al., 2024, §3.2 / Figure 3](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.02660v1#S3.F3); [§2.1 / Figure 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.02660v1#S2.F1) likewise shows that using only long data hurts downstream long-context performance despite better perplexity.

The OLMo 2 7B average 53.0 → 62.9 concerns mid-training on selected high-quality data using 5–10% of FLOPs; it is not an isolated causal effect of long context ([OLMo 2, Table 9](https://arxiv.org/html/2501.00656)). The stage blocks formerly shown here had equal visual widths only to indicate order, not equal training durations or token budgets.

We can now summarize the section: require distant links, practice them at increasing distances, and reserve a measured share of the mixture for long data. The next unit of training data will be a trajectory of actions in an environment.
:::

## Interaction trajectories and synthetic environments {#frontier-f19 .fv-slide background-color="#ffffff"}

```{=html}
<div class="fv-meta"><span class="fv-id">D 25 / 42</span><span class="fv-cluster">Architecture</span><span class="fv-cluster active">Data</span><span class="fv-cluster">Training</span><span class="fv-cluster">Inference</span><span class="fv-cluster">Tools</span></div>
<div class="fv-body f19-body">
  <div class="f19-head"><div>Environment specifications<br><span>+ Initial states</span></div><div>Independent trajectories</div><div>Recorded outcomes</div></div>
  <div class="f19-trajectory"><div class="f19-seed">env A · state a₀</div><div class="f19-tape"><span>Observation</span><i>→</i><span>Action</span><i>→</i><span>Result</span></div><div class="f19-outcome">completed</div></div>
  <div class="f19-trajectory"><div class="f19-seed">env B · state b₀</div><div class="f19-tape"><span>Observation</span><i>→</i><span class="fragment fv-highlight" data-fragment-index="1">Action</span><i>→</i><span class="fragment fv-highlight" data-fragment-index="1">Result</span><i>→</i><span>…</span></div><div class="f19-outcome">recovered</div></div>
  <div class="f19-trajectory"><div class="f19-seed">env C · state c₀</div><div class="f19-tape"><span>Observation</span><i>→</i><span>Action</span><i>→</i><span>Result</span><i>→</i><span>…</span><i>→</i><span>Result</span></div><div class="f19-outcome">timeout</div></div>
  <div class="f19-detail fragment" data-fragment-index="1"><b>One recorded step</b><code>Action: run(test)</code><i>→</i><code>Result: exit 1 + error log</code></div>
  <div class="f19-process"><span>Generation</span><i>→</i><span>Execution</span><i>→</i><span>Logging</span><i>→</i><span>Selection</span></div>
</div>
<div class="fv-takeaway">The corpus preserves actions, observed results, and the course of the interaction.</div>
<div class="fv-source"><a href="https://arxiv.org/html/2607.24653v1#S4.SS2">Kimi K3, §4.2, 2026</a> · <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629">ReAct, 2022</a> · Teaching diagram</div>
```

::: {.notes}
A correct final answer alone is not enough to train tool interaction. We need to know what the agent observed, which action it chose, and what the environment actually returned. The unit of data therefore becomes a trajectory: a sequence of these steps.

The left column specifies the environment conditions and initial state. The three rows are independent: they represent separate episodes. Observation is what the agent can see, action is what it does, and result is the execution outcome. The result becomes part of the next observation and shapes what happens next.

The right column records different outcomes: completion, recovery from an error, and termination at a limit. The final status alone does not tell us how the agent got there.

*First click: reveal a specific recorded step.*

The agent ran a test. The environment returned exit code one and an error log. If we keep only the intention, "run the test," we lose the actual observation that should explain the next step.

The bottom chain shows data collection: candidate generation, execution, event logging, and selection. A useful episode may contain a failed attempt followed by recovery. Whether we retain an error therefore depends on the purpose of the data. For now, we are deciding what to record; how to train on that record is a separate choice. Let us examine a small file interaction where the distinction between action, result, and state is directly visible.

**Sources:** [Kimi K3, §4.2, 2026](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.24653v1#S4.SS2), [ReAct, 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629).
:::

## Trajectory record: preserve failure and recovery {#frontier-f19-detail .fv-slide .fv-detail background-color="#ffffff"}

```{=html}
<div class="fv-meta"><span class="fv-id">D 26 / 42</span><span class="fv-cluster">Architecture</span><span class="fv-cluster active">Data</span><span class="fv-cluster">Training</span><span class="fv-cluster">Inference</span><span class="fv-cluster">Tools</span></div>
<div class="fv-body d19-body">
  <div class="d19-goal"><b>Environment specification:</b> result.txt must contain the string <code>42</code>.<br><span>Initial state: no file. Observation is the part of the state available to the agent.</span></div>
  <table class="d19-log"><thead><tr><th>Step</th><th>Observation</th><th>Action</th><th>Result / next observation</th><th>done</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>0</td><td>File not checked</td><td><code>read("result.txt")</code></td><td><code>ENOENT</code> · no file</td><td>false</td></tr><tr class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1"><td>1</td><td>No file</td><td><code>write("result.txt", "42")</code></td><td><code>ok</code> · verifier: content = 42</td><td>true</td></tr></tbody></table>
  <div class="d19-transition fragment" data-fragment-index="1"><div><b>Failure</b><span>File absent → absent</span></div><div><b>Recovery</b><span>File absent → contains 42</span></div><div><b>Log</b><span>Preserves both transitions</span></div></div>
  <div class="d19-selection fragment" data-fragment-index="2"><div><b>Episode selection rule</b><code>goal_verified &amp;&amp; log_complete</code></div><div><b>Keep trajectory: [step 0, step 1]</b><span>The error provides context for recovery.<br>Keeping a record ≠ choosing a training signal.</span></div></div>
</div>
<div class="fv-takeaway">A full trajectory shows how the agent reached a verified goal, including failure and recovery.</div>
<div class="fv-source"><a href="https://gymnasium.farama.org/api/env/">Gymnasium: step / observation / termination</a> · <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629">ReAct, 2022</a> · Teaching protocol</div>
```

::: {.notes}
The environment has a simple goal: result.txt must contain the string "42". Initially, the file does not exist. The collection system knows that state, but the agent receives only observations and has not yet checked whether the file exists. This distinguishes the state of the world from the information available to the agent.

At step zero, the agent calls the file-reading tool. The result, ENOENT, means the file does not exist. The failed read leaves the file system unchanged, but the agent's observation changes: the absence of the file is now known. The done field, which indicates whether the episode has ended, is still false.

*First click: show the recovery and state transitions.*

At the next step, the agent writes the string "42". The environment confirms execution, and the verifier checks the contents. The goal has been reached, so done becomes true in our protocol. The external state has now changed too: the file exists with the required contents. The log preserves both transitions.

*Second click: reveal the selection rule.*

The rule requires both a verified goal and a complete log. Both conditions are met, so we keep steps zero and one. The failed read explains the subsequent recovery. Removing it would discard part of the decision context.

But recording an action does not mean training the model to repeat it. An error can remain as context while the training signal is assigned separately. Similarly, stopping at a limit must not be treated as achieving the goal.

The file episode showed what to record about an interaction. Next, we examine a published DeepSeek-V3.2 example that creates the environment, tools, task, and verifier together. We will then check whether training in such environments helped on other tasks.

**Optional detail.** The done field is simplified for this teaching table. For example, Gymnasium distinguishes natural termination from a cutoff imposed by an external limit using terminated and truncated. Keeping a full trajectory does not define the loss function or automatically imply reinforcement learning: the data format and training algorithm are separate choices.

**Optional comprehension check.** After the failed read, did the environment state change, or the agent's observation? The file is still absent, but the agent has learned this. The step result is what connects the next action to the information available to the agent.

**Sources:** [Gymnasium: step / observation / termination](https://gymnasium.farama.org/api/env/), [ReAct, 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629).
:::

## Agent data: task, environment, and verification {#frontier-f19-case .fv-slide background-color="#ffffff"}

```{=html}
<div class="fv-meta"><span class="fv-id">D 27 / 42</span><span class="fv-cluster">Architecture</span><span class="fv-cluster active">Data</span><span class="fv-cluster">Training</span><span class="fv-cluster">Inference</span><span class="fv-cluster">Tools</span></div>
<div class="fv-body dc-body">
  <div class="dc-kicker"><b>DeepSeek-V3.2 · 〈environment, tools, task, verifier〉</b><span>Published example · PDF p.12</span></div>
  <div class="dc-trip">
    <div><h3>Trip on October 1–3, 2025</h3><div class="dc-constraints"><div><b>No repeats:</b> cities, hotels, restaurants or attractions.</div><div><b>One city per day:</b> hotel, both restaurants and attraction must be in that day’s city.</div></div></div>
    <div><h3>Tools from the same task</h3><div class="dc-tools">get_all_cities()<br>get_all_hotels_by_city(city)<br>submit_result(answer_text)<br>…</div><div class="dc-answer dc-highlight"><b>verifier checks the constraints of the answer</b></div></div>
  </div>
  <div class="dc-dataset"><span><b>1,827</b> environments</span><span aria-hidden="true">·</span><span><b>4,417</b> tasks</span></div>
</div>
<div class="fv-takeaway">The reference solution uses tools; the verifier checks the task constraints.</div>
<div class="fv-source"><a href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.02556#page=12">DeepSeek-V3.2, §3.2.3, example on p.12, 2025</a> · Conditions and tools abridged; additional task details in speaker notes</div>
```

::: {.notes}
The file example already had a state, actions, and a verifiable goal. DeepSeek-V3.2 scales the creation of these conditions: in its general-agent dataset, the unit of data comprises an environment, tools, a task, and a verifier. After selection for nonzero pass@100, the authors obtain 1,827 synthetic environments and 4,417 tasks. At least one of one hundred attempts must succeed. This selects solvable tasks; it does not require the agent to succeed every time.

Let us examine the published PDF example, rather than inventing a task. The agent must plan a three-day trip starting in Hangzhou. Cities and selected venues must not repeat, and all locations on each day must be in that day's city. The hotel price on day two determines additional requirements. One exact branch is: if the hotel costs at least 800 yuan, the two restaurants must cost less than 350 in total, each must have a rating of at least 4.0, and the attraction must cost less than 120.

The original also includes branches for the 500–800 and 200–500 yuan ranges. They are omitted for readability, as the caption explicitly states. The text does not formalize the boundaries of those ranges, so we do not redefine them.

The right column lists three actual tools; others include get_infos_by_hotel(info_keywords, hotel), get_all_restaurants_by_city(city) and get_all_attractions_by_city(city). The answer fields are time, city, hotel, afternoon_restaurant, afternoon_attraction and evening_restaurant. There are also tools for retrieving details about restaurants and attractions. The reference solution must use the tool interface; direct database access is prohibited. The result is submitted as a JSON array of three objects through submit_result(answer_text), and the verifier checks it.

Creating an environment does not by itself establish that training on it is useful. The next slide examines transfer to external agent tasks.

**Sources:** [DeepSeek-V3.2, §3.2.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.02556#S3.SS2.SSS3), [full published example, PDF p.12](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.02556#page=12). The HTML version omits the box containing the full example, so the conditions were taken from the PDF.
:::

## Training in synthetic environments transfers to other tasks {#frontier-f19-experiment .fv-slide .fv-detail background-color="#ffffff"}

```{=html}
<div class="fv-meta"><span class="fv-id">D 28 / 42</span><span class="fv-cluster">Architecture</span><span class="fv-cluster active">Data</span><span class="fv-cluster">Training</span><span class="fv-cluster">Inference</span><span class="fv-cluster">Tools</span></div>
<div class="fv-body dc-body">
  <div class="dc-kicker"><b>DeepSeek-V3.2 · external test of tool use</b><span>Experiment · §4.3, Figure 5</span></div>
  <div class="dc-evidence dc-transfer">
    <figure class="dc-figure"><img src="assets/data_cases_20261007/deepseek-figure5-tau2-overall.png" alt="Original τ²-bench Overall panel from Figure 5: SFT about 55 percent, synthetic RL about 83 percent"><figcaption>τ²-bench / Overall: external agent-task benchmark. Blue: RL;<br>green dashed: SFT; black: Exp. <a href="assets/data_cases_20261007/deepseek-figure5-original.png">Full Figure 5</a>.</figcaption></figure>
    <div class="dc-aside">
      <div class="dc-highlight"><div class="dc-number">≈55% → ≈83%</div><p>SFT: learning from examples.<br>RL: learning from rewards.</p></div>
      <p><b>During RL:</b> only synthetic general-agent tasks from this process.</p>
      <p><b>Non-thinking mode:</b> other RL data and long reasoning excluded.</p>
      <small>Approximate values read from the plot.<br>A separate ablation, not the final run.</small>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>
<div class="fv-takeaway">The synthetic dataset's value is tested through transfer to an external agent benchmark.</div>
<div class="fv-source"><a href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.02556#page=16">DeepSeek-V3.2, §4.3, Figure 5, p.16</a> · Original panel; ≈55% and ≈83% estimated from the plot</div>
```

::: {.notes}
The final case adds a test of transfer. SFT learns from examples of correct behavior; RL learns from a reward signal for the result. We will examine these algorithms in the next section; for now, distinguishing the two stages is enough. In Section 4.3 of DeepSeek-V3.2, the authors take an SFT model and run RL only on synthetic general-agent tasks. The external τ²-bench tests agent tasks involving tools; these are separate from the training environments just generated. The authors use non-thinking mode to isolate the effect of this dataset from long reasoning and other RL data.

The slide shows the original τ²-bench Overall panel from Figure 5. The green dashed line marks the SFT baseline at about 55%. The blue curve shows performance as RL proceeds, reaching about 83% by the end. These are visual estimates from the plot, hence the approximation signs. The black dashed line is the additional Exp line from the original; the main conclusion here relies on the comparison with SFT.

We do not present this experiment as the performance of the full released DeepSeek-V3.2, or claim that different training methods were compared at equal budgets. The supported claim is narrower: training on this synthetic dataset improved performance on external agent tasks under the stated conditions.

The last direction of Part I: removing an unwanted record and constructing an example of safe behavior are different tasks.

**Source:** [DeepSeek-V3.2, §4.3, Figure 5, PDF p.16](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.02556#page=16). The [full Figure 5](assets/data_cases_20261007/deepseek-figure5-original.png) is saved locally. The values ≈55% and ≈83% are approximate readings from the Overall panel.
:::

## Safety data is not just filtered data {#data-safety .fv-slide background-color="#ffffff"}

```{=html}
<div class="fv-meta"><span class="fv-id">D 29 / 42</span><span class="fv-cluster">Architecture</span><span class="fv-cluster active">Data</span><span class="fv-cluster">Training</span><span class="fv-cluster">Inference</span><span class="fv-cluster">Tools</span></div>
<div class="fv-body d25-body">
  <div class="d25-process d25-filter-process">
    <h3>FILTER THE CORPUS</h3>
    <div class="d25-flow d25-corpus-flow">
      <div class="d25-documents" role="img" aria-label="A stack of source documents, an unwanted record and a selected corpus">
        <span class="d25-sheet d25-sheet-back" aria-hidden="true"></span>
        <span class="d25-sheet d25-sheet-middle" aria-hidden="true"></span>
        <div class="d25-sheet d25-sheet-front"><span>Source corpus</span><i aria-hidden="true"></i><i aria-hidden="true"></i></div>
        <div class="d25-discard">Unwanted record <span aria-hidden="true">×</span></div>
      </div>
      <div class="fv-arrow" aria-hidden="true">→</div>
      <div class="d25-filter">
        <svg viewBox="0 0 120 80" width="120" height="80" role="img" aria-label="Corpus filter"><path d="M8 10H112L73 48V69L47 76V48Z" fill="var(--fv-soft)" stroke="var(--fv-ink)" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M26 25H94" stroke="var(--fv-line)" stroke-width="2"/></svg>
        <span>Select records</span>
      </div>
      <div class="fv-arrow" aria-hidden="true">→</div>
      <div class="d25-corpus"><b>Selected corpus</b><div class="d25-kept-docs" aria-hidden="true"><span><i></i><i></i><i></i></span><span><i></i><i></i><i></i></span><span><i></i><i></i><i></i></span></div></div>
    </div>
    <p class="d25-question">Which records should remain?</p>
  </div>
  <div class="d25-process d25-behavior-process fragment" data-fragment-index="1">
    <h3>CONSTRUCT BEHAVIOR EXAMPLES <span>Illustrative teaching example</span></h3>
    <div class="d25-flow d25-behavior-flow">
      <div class="d25-dialogue">
        <div class="d25-request fragment d25-context" data-fragment-index="2"><span class="d25-label">USER REQUEST</span><p>Help me get access to someone else’s account.</p></div>
        <div class="d25-response"><span class="d25-label">ASSISTANT RESPONSE</span><div class="d25-response-slot">
          <div class="d25-unsafe"><b>UNSAFE RESPONSE</b><p>[Assistance with unauthorized access]</p></div>
          <div class="d25-safe"><b>SAFE RESPONSE</b><p>I can’t help access someone else’s account.</p><p>For your own account, use official account recovery.</p></div>
        </div></div>
      </div>
      <div class="fv-arrow fragment" data-fragment-index="2" aria-hidden="true">→</div>
      <div class="d25-revision fragment" data-fragment-index="2"><b>Critique<br>+ revise</b><span>Replace the answer</span><em class="fragment" data-fragment-index="2">Request = context<br>for the right response</em></div>
      <div class="fv-arrow fragment" data-fragment-index="2" aria-hidden="true">→</div>
      <div class="d25-target fragment" data-fragment-index="2">
        <span class="d25-target-label">TARGET PAIR</span>
        <div class="d25-dialogue">
          <div class="d25-request fragment d25-context" data-fragment-index="2"><span class="d25-label">USER REQUEST</span><p>Help me get access to someone else’s account.</p></div>
          <div class="d25-response"><span class="d25-label">ASSISTANT RESPONSE</span><div class="d25-response-slot"><div class="d25-safe"><b>SAFE RESPONSE</b><p>I can’t help access someone else’s account.</p><p>For your own account, use official account recovery.</p></div></div></div>
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>
    <p class="d25-question">How should the assistant respond here?</p>
  </div>
</div>
<div class="fv-takeaway fragment" data-fragment-index="3">Keep the challenging situation. Change the desired response.</div>
<div class="fv-source"><a href="https://www.anthropic.com/research/constitutional-ai-harmlessness-from-ai-feedback">Anthropic, Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback, 2022</a> · Supervised phase: response → critique → revision</div>
```

::: {.notes}
Removing unwanted material and preparing examples of acceptable behavior solve different problems. Corpus filtering asks which records should remain. Constructing a behavior example asks which situation to show the model and what response to set as the desired target. A challenging request can therefore remain in the input while an unsafe answer is replaced.

**On opening: FILTER THE CORPUS.** The diagram distinguishes source records from the selected corpus. Filtering policies depend on the corpus and its purpose; the scheme does not imply that all sensitive material must be removed from pre-training.

**First click: compare the unsafe and safe answers.** The request asks for access to someone else’s account. The unsafe placeholder contains no technical instructions; the safe response refuses unauthorized access and offers official recovery for the user’s own account. This is an illustrative teaching example, not a verbatim example from Constitutional AI.

**Second click: critique and revise, then retain the target pair.** A lime frame highlights the unchanged request in both dialogue cards. It supplies the context in which the desired response should be learned; its presence does not make the request an instruction to fulfill. This is the same principle as the trajectory slide: the failed file read stayed as context while the next action was the target. Context is not the training target; technically, this is the loss masking mentioned on the trajectory overview. Keeping the challenging situation and changing the desired response is different from removing the entire record. The slide illustrates target construction; the exact loss and token masking depend on the training implementation.

In the supervised phase of Constitutional AI, the authors sample responses from an initial model, generate critiques according to constitutional principles, revise the responses, and fine-tune on the revised responses. The distinction we take from the reference is between the initial model answer and the revised answer used as training material. The paper also has a separate reinforcement-learning phase using AI feedback; this diagram illustrates the supervised revision principle rather than the complete method.

**Third click: the takeaway.** Keep the challenging situation and change the desired response. How much does such data weigh? The next slide measures it.

**Source:** [Anthropic, Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback, December 15, 2022](https://www.anthropic.com/research/constitutional-ai-harmlessness-from-ai-feedback). The filtering scheme, account-access example, and comparison of unsafe and safe responses are original illustrations.

[DALL·E 2](https://openai.com/index/dall-e-2-pre-training-mitigations/) describes image filtering and its potential bias; [Sora 2](https://deploymentsafety.openai.com/sora-2/specific-risk-areas-mitigations) distinguishes corpus processing from deployment safeguards. NSFW and CSAM are distinct categories. [Lyria 3.5](https://deepmind.google/models/model-cards/lyria-3-5/) separately lists deduplication, safety and quality filtering: audio-signal quality, lyric safety, desired behavior examples and product moderation solve different problems, and filtering can alter the corpus composition.
:::

## Safety data is small, but later stages erode it {#data-safety-evidence .fv-slide .fv-detail background-color="#ffffff"}

```{=html}

<div class="fv-source"><a href="https://arxiv.org/html/2411.15124v5">Tülu 3, Tables 10 and 25, 2024</a> · <a href="https://huggingface.co/allenai/OLMoE-1B-7B-0125-Instruct">OLMoE-1B-7B-0125-Instruct model card</a> · Higher is better for every score</div>
```

::: {.notes}
Constitutional AI showed how a safety example is built. Tülu 3 measures how much such data matters. Removing the safety data from the SFT mixture drops the safety average from 93.1 to 74.7, while the average over the other tasks moves only from 64.1 to 63.7. The authors call safety orthogonal: a small slice of data carries it.

**First click: follow safety through training.** The safety average is 93.1 after SFT, 87.2 after DPO and 85.5 after final RL. Two opposite shifts hide inside this number: XSTest rises from 90.4 to 93.3, so needless refusals become rarer, while the DAN jailbreak score falls from 88.3 to 62.0. Safety data therefore belongs in every stage, not only one.

**Second click: OLMoE.** With the same base model, changing only post-training raises safety from 51.4 to 90.4.

Coverage matters too: Karpathy explains Base64 jailbreaks by refusal data that is mostly in English. The next slide closes Part I by returning to the cover riddle.

**Sources:** [Tülu 3, Tables 10 and 25](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.15124v5); [OLMoE model card](https://huggingface.co/allenai/OLMoE-1B-7B-0125-Instruct).
:::

::: {.notes}
Back to the cover riddle: same model, same budget, plus 6.5 Core points. Table 12 splits them into two steps.

**First click: the two steps.** Plus 2.0 from C4 to RedPajama, where curated sources are mixed into web data, and plus 4.5 from RedPajama to DCLM-baseline, where the model-based quality filter is the main ingredient. RedPajama differs from C4 in more than curated sources, so read the labels as the main ingredient of each step.

**Second click: the twist.** Table 6 adds the same curated sources on top of DCLM-baseline and loses 1.2 points. Once filtering is good, a source with a "high-quality" name can hurt. Table 6 reports DCLM-baseline at 31.1 rather than Table 12's 30.2, a different run, so we show only the difference.

**Third click: the takeaway.** The progress column marks all seven Part I sections complete and Part II as future. The rules behind it remain: Practitioners describe progress as bricks: Ai2 speaks of improvements worth 2–5% each, every one checked by a cheap experiment. Change one thing at a time with the model and tokens fixed. Judge by downstream tasks, not by loss. Repetition is a weight you set on purpose; when unique data runs out, rephrase. Human agreement and uniqueness are not the same as quality.

This closes Part I. Part II applies the same rules to images and video: selection, rewriting the supervision, synthetic data with a checkable answer, and what changes when the example has a time axis.

**Sources:** [DataComp-LM, Tables 6 and 12](https://arxiv.org/html/2406.11794v4).
:::

**First click.** The bird query and its two matches receive emphasis first; the flower query and its two matches follow in the same reveal. Unrelated candidates fade. The two inputs to VISUAL RETRIEVAL are query images and candidate images. Matching uses visual representations, not a requirement for paired captions. Reduced motion shows the completed selection directly.

**Second click.** Four retrieved images join the four seeds in the final frame. Solid and dashed borders distinguish their origins; all final cards have the same size. The near-copy stays outside. This is an outcome illustration, not an algorithmic ordering: DINOv2 deduplicates its uncurated pool before retrieval and also removes benchmark near-copies. The paper combines curated sources and retrieved images. We omit index, clustering and neighbor-count settings.

The next example keeps an image fixed and improves its textual supervision.

Source: [DINOv2, §3, Figure 3, Appendix A](https://arxiv.org/html/2304.07193v2).

```{=html}
</div>

```

::: {.notes}
The photograph and both short caption texts come from the left example in BLIP Figure 4. The photo is extracted unchanged from the PDF image stream. Initially only the web caption appears.

**First click.** Reveal the generated caption and the image–text filter. The source figure colors its web text red and synthetic text green: the web caption is rejected and the generated caption is kept. These are the authors' decisions for this example, not a new judgment by us. CapFilt generates candidates and filters both original and synthetic texts. A generated caption is not automatically accepted; the other examples in the paper include rejected synthetic text.

**Second click.** Reveal a separate HUMAN OBSERVATION route from PixMo-Cap: look, speak, transcribe, edit. People describe what they see; a speech-to-text system transcribes their recordings; a language-only LLM consolidates or edits the transcripts. This lower route is independent of BLIP. No arrow connects the two workflows. In the upper route a model proposes an image description; in the lower route language editing works from human observation. The photo remains unchanged throughout.

This is rewriting from Part I, now for images: the knowledge in the pixels stays, the supervision around it improves. Next, we follow one musical track through several kinds of annotation, then examine how a short generator prompt is expanded. After those two examples, we generate an image and its answer from a program.

Sources: [BLIP, §3.3 and Figure 4](https://arxiv.org/html/2201.12086v2); [PixMo-Cap, §3 and Appendix F](https://arxiv.org/html/2409.17146v2).
:::

::: {.notes}
Our fictional track aligns all annotations on one time axis. On click one reveal the caption and structured sound attributes; on click two reveal lyrics and musical notes together. MiniMax Music3 documents three caption components: global metadata, vocal details and arrangement. Lyria 3.5 documents captions at several detail levels. These describe sound, rather than transcribing its words or pitch events.

The YuE2 pipeline separately obtains lyrics with ASR and symbolic music with transcription. The dashed word is an invented ambiguity (‘light’ versus ‘night’). An ASR error affects the lyric target but does not establish an error in an independently produced note sequence. Symbolic transcription can also be uncertain and is not necessarily the original composer's score. Provenance, timing and confidence should be retained per annotation. We do not attribute a lyric-ASR cover workflow to MiniMax, whose selected card does not establish it.

**Source disclosures (speaker detail).** The selected Suno v6 announcement names WMG, BMG and Believe; YuE2 Table 12 reports approximately 346,000 hours for YuE2 itself; the Lyria 3.5 card describes audio, captions and processing. These are different disclosure axes. A disclosure missing from one selected document cannot be treated as absent from every publication, and developer statements are not an independent audit of the complete corpus. This connects the annotation example to what is actually documented about musical training data. Next, consider how detailed training descriptions relate to an expanded generator prompt.

Sources (checked 21 October 2026): [Suno v6](https://suno.com/blog/introducing-v6); [MiniMax structured captions](https://huggingface.co/MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-Music3); [Lyria data](https://deepmind.google/models/model-cards/lyria-3-5/); [YuE2 §3 / Appendix C](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.33757v1).
:::
